title: Going round: what keeps a thing in a circle, and why it flies off straight when the pull stops

summary.text: Whirl a small bag on a string, and your fingers feel the string pulling inward the whole time. Whirl it twice as fast, and the pull is not twice as big but about four times as big. Let go, and the bag does not curve away. It flies off in a straight line. A stone on a string, a car on a bend, wet clothes in a spin dryer and the Moon going round the Earth all need a pull towards the middle, every moment. The pull must grow with the mass, with the square of the speed, and as the circle gets tighter. The 'outward push' you feel on a bend is your own body trying to go straight, and scientists still argue about whether to call it a force.
summary.art: A girl in a hall whirling a small cloth bag on a string around her hand, with a dotted straight line showing where the bag would fly if the string were let go.

intro.hook: Whirl a small bag on a string. Your fingers feel a pull, and the faster you whirl, the stronger the pull gets. Now let go. Does the bag fly straight on, curve round, or go outward? Nobody pushes the bag outward, so why do you feel a pull at all?
intro.text: The string pulls the bag towards your hand all the time. That pull bends the bag's path into a circle. When the pull stops, the bag goes straight on. In this unit you measure how the pull changes with speed, you slide coins off a turntable, and you watch a spin dryer throw water out through its holes. You find out why a car slows for a bend, why a lab spins blood and a dairy spins milk, and why the Moon keeps falling towards the Earth without ever getting closer.
intro.art: A cloth bag on a string whirling around a pen held in a child's hand, with a few coins hanging from the other end of the string.

outcomes: I can explain that a thing going round needs a pull towards the middle all the time, and that without it, the thing flies off in a straight line.
I can run a fair test with a whirler, record the turns in a table, and say how the speed of the circling changes when the pull changes.
I can say how the pull needed changes when the speed doubles, when the circle gets wider, and when the mass gets bigger.
I can explain why coins on a turntable slide off from the edge first, and why a heavy coin and a light coin slide off together.
I can explain how a spin dryer, a cream separator and a laboratory centrifuge use the same idea.
I can explain why a car slows for a bend, why roads and railway lines are tilted at bends, and why a cyclist leans.
I can explain that the Moon keeps falling towards the Earth without getting closer, and say what scientists argue about when they say 'centrifugal force'.

terms.meaning: Moving round and round in a circle. A thing in circular motion changes its direction every moment.
terms.example: A stone whirled on a string, and a car going round a roundabout, are in circular motion.
terms.art: A stone on a string moving in a circle, with small arrows along the circle showing the changing direction.

terms.meaning: The middle point of a circle. Every point on the circle is the same distance from it.
terms.example: The centre of a merry-go-round is the post in the middle.
terms.art: A merry-go-round seen from above with a dot at the centre and a line to the edge.

terms.meaning: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge. A small radius means a tight circle, and a big radius means a wide circle.
terms.example: A string 40 centimetres long makes a circle with a radius of 40 centimetres.
terms.art: A circle with a line from the centre to the edge labelled radius, and a tape measure beside it.

terms.meaning: A straight line that just touches a circle at one point, and points the way a thing on the circle is moving at that moment.
terms.example: Sparks from a grinding wheel fly off along tangents.
terms.art: A circle with a straight line touching it at one point and a spark flying along that line.

terms.meaning: The pull or push towards the centre that keeps a thing going round. The word means 'centre-seeking'. It is not a new kind of force. It is a name for whatever force points to the middle.
terms.example: The string pulling a whirled bag, and the Earth's gravity pulling the Moon, are both centripetal forces.
terms.art: A bag whirling on a string with an arrow along the string pointing towards the hand at the centre.

terms.meaning: The name many people give to the feeling of being pushed outward when you turn. Scientists agree that something is felt, and they still discuss whether it should be called a force.
terms.example: On a sharp bend in a bus, you feel pressed against the window on the outside of the turn.
terms.art: A girl in a bus pressed gently against the side window as the bus turns.

terms.meaning: The way every thing keeps doing what it is doing. A moving thing goes in a straight line at the same speed until a force changes it.
terms.example: A coin on a spinning turntable wants to go straight on, and slides off when the friction is not enough.
terms.art: A coin leaving the edge of a turntable along a straight line.

terms.meaning: The pull along a string, a rope or a wire when it is stretched tight.
terms.example: The string of a whirled bag has tension.
terms.art: A taut string with a bag at one end and a hand at the other, with arrows pointing along the string.

terms.meaning: The grip between two surfaces that touch. It works against sliding.
terms.example: Friction between a tyre and the road gives a car the pull it needs to take a bend.
terms.art: A car tyre on a road with a small arrow pointing inward at the contact point on a bend.

terms.meaning: The pull between things because they have mass. The Earth's gravity pulls everything towards the ground, and holds the Moon in its path.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a dropped tumbler down, and holds the Moon near the Earth.
terms.art: The Earth with an arrow of gravity pulling the Moon and a stone.

terms.meaning: The path of one thing going round another because of gravity.
terms.example: The Moon is in orbit round the Earth, and the Earth is in orbit round the Sun.
terms.art: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon, with a ring showing each orbit.

terms.meaning: How much matter a thing has. More mass means a bigger pull is needed to turn it.
terms.example: A heavy stone on a string pulls harder on your hand than a light one at the same speed.
terms.art: A heavy stone and a light bag whirling on equal strings, with a longer arrow for the heavy stone.

terms.meaning: One full trip round a circle, back to the start. Scientists also say a revolution.
terms.example: A bag that goes round 10 times in 10 seconds makes one turn every second.
terms.art: A bag on a string with a dotted circle and a counter showing 1, 2 and 3 turns.

terms.meaning: A machine that spins things fast, so that heavier parts of a mixture move to the outside and lighter parts stay near the middle.
terms.example: A laboratory centrifuge spins tubes of blood to separate the blood cells from the liquid.
terms.art: A laboratory centrifuge with test tubes, in which the heavier part has settled at the outer end of each tube.

terms.meaning: A bend in a road or a rail that is tilted, with the outside edge higher than the inside edge, so that part of the push of the ground points towards the middle.
terms.example: On many railway curves, the outer rail is raised a little.
terms.art: A railway curve seen end-on, with the outer rail higher than the inner rail and a train leaning slightly in.

terms.meaning: How far a thing moves in a certain time, such as metres every second.
terms.example: A bag that goes round a circle 2 metres long in 1 second has a speed of 2 metres per second.
terms.art: A bag on a circle with a stopwatch showing 1 second and an arrow of its speed.

explanations.concept: Going round needs a pull towards the middle, all the time
explanations.definition: A thing moving in a circle changes its direction every moment. A force that points towards the middle of the circle makes this happen. Scientists call it the centripetal force.
explanations.description: Think of the bag on the string. Because of inertia, the bag wants to go straight on. The string pulls it towards your hand at every moment, and that bends its path into a circle. The pull always points at a right angle to the way the bag is moving. So it changes the direction of the bag, but it does not make the bag faster or slower. Different things give the pull. A string gives tension. A road gives friction to a car on a bend. The Earth gives gravity to the Moon. The wall of a spin dryer gives a push to the clothes. The word 'centripetal' only names what the pull does: it seeks the middle. It is not a new kind of force.
examples: The string pulls a whirled bag towards your hand.
The friction of the tyres pulls a car round a bend.
The Earth's gravity pulls the Moon, so that the Moon goes round the Earth.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a whirled bag with a string arrow to the centre, a car on a bend with a tyre arrow to the centre, and the Moon with a gravity arrow to the Earth.
explanations.context: This card gives the main idea of the unit: a thing going round needs a pull towards the middle.

explanations.concept: Without the pull, a thing flies off in a straight line
explanations.definition: When the pull towards the middle stops, a thing moves in a straight line, along the way it was going at that moment. This line just touches the circle, and is called a tangent.
explanations.description: A common guess is that a whirled stone, when let go, flies outward from the middle, like the spoke of a wheel. But it does not. It goes along the tangent, in the direction it was moving. Sparks from a grinding wheel fly off in long straight lines. Mud thrown from a tyre leaves in a straight line. Drops fly off a spun wet umbrella in straight lines. A hammer thrower in an athletics match lets go of the hammer when it is moving towards the field, not when it is pointing at it. Each time, the thing is doing what the first law says: going straight, because no force is bending its path any more.
examples: Sparks fly off in straight lines from a grinding wheel.
Mud flies off a fast tyre along the way the tyre was turning.
Water drops leave a spun wet umbrella in straight lines.
explanations.art: A circle with a stone moving round it, and three straight lines at different points showing where the stone would go if let go there.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens when the pull towards the middle stops.

explanations.concept: A faster circle needs a much bigger pull
explanations.definition: In the same circle, going twice as fast needs four times the pull. Going three times as fast needs nine times the pull.
explanations.description: A faster thing has to turn round more quickly, and it also has more speed to bend every second. The two effects multiply, so the pull grows with the square of the speed. In the whirler test, you used 4 coins, 8 coins and 16 coins as the pull. Four times the coins did not need four times the turns. It needed only about twice the turns. So twice the speed needed four times the pull. A car going round a bend at 40 kilometres an hour needs four times the grip of the same car at 20 kilometres an hour. That is why a small increase in speed can suddenly be too much for a bend.
examples: Four times the coins held the whirled bag at about twice the turns in the same time.
A car at 40 kilometres an hour needs four times as much grip on a bend as at 20 kilometres an hour.
A merry-go-round that turns twice as fast needs four times the holding force on the riders.
explanations.art: Two whirlers side by side: one with 4 coins hanging and the bag going round slowly, and one with 16 coins hanging and the bag going round twice as fast.
explanations.context: This card is about how the pull changes when the speed changes.

explanations.concept: A tighter circle needs a bigger pull
explanations.definition: At the same speed, a circle with half the radius needs twice the pull.
explanations.description: A tight circle turns the direction more sharply at every moment than a wide one, so it needs more pull. A car can take a wide bend at 40 kilometres an hour, but a sharp hairpin bend on a ghat road needs a much lower speed, such as 15 or 20. On the same turntable, a coin near the middle goes round a small circle, and needs less friction to stay on than a coin near the edge, which goes round a bigger circle and also moves faster. That is why the coin at the edge slides off first.
examples: Road signs at hairpin bends on ghat roads tell drivers to slow down.
A coin near the edge of a turntable slides off before a coin near the middle.
A cycle taking a sharp turn must lean more than one taking a wide turn at the same speed.
explanations.art: A coin near the middle and a coin near the edge of a turntable, with a longer arrow on the outer coin.
explanations.context: This card is about how the pull changes when the circle gets smaller or bigger.

explanations.concept: More mass needs a bigger pull, and the rule in one line
explanations.definition: The pull needed for a circle is the mass times the speed times the speed, divided by the radius. A bigger mass needs a bigger pull in the same proportion.
explanations.description: This comes from Newton's second law. A bigger mass needs a bigger force to change its motion. A stone of 0.2 kilograms whirled at 5 metres per second on a 1 metre string needs a pull of 0.2 x 5 x 5 divided by 1, which is 5 newtons. A child of 30 kilograms on a roundabout of radius 2 metres, going at 2 metres per second, needs a holding force of 30 x 2 x 2 divided by 2, which is 60 newtons. The rule says three things in one line: more mass needs more pull, more speed needs much more pull, and a bigger radius needs less.
examples: A stone of 0.2 kilograms at 5 metres per second on a 1 metre string needs 5 newtons.
A child of 30 kilograms at 2 metres per second on a roundabout of radius 2 metres needs 60 newtons.
A heavy lorry on a bend needs more grip from its tyres than a car at the same speed.
explanations.art: A formula card showing mass, speed and radius with three arrows: bigger mass, bigger pull; bigger speed, much bigger pull; bigger radius, smaller pull.
explanations.context: This card puts all three changes into one rule, and gives numbers.

explanations.concept: The outward feeling on a bend is your own body going straight
explanations.definition: When a vehicle turns, your body tries to keep going straight. The seat, door or rail pushes you inward. What you feel is that push on your body, and your body pressing back because of its inertia.
explanations.description: In a bus going round a bend, you feel pressed against the window on the outside of the turn. No force is pushing you outward. Your body was going straight, and the bus turned under you. The window is the thing that pushes you inward, and bends your path into the curve. If the window suddenly vanished, you would not fly outward. You would carry on in a straight line, while the bus turned away. On a merry-go-round, the bar pushes inward on your back, and what you feel is your body pressing on the bar.
examples: In a bus on a left bend, you lean towards the right side.
On a merry-go-round, you press on the bar that holds you in.
In a car that turns sharply, a school bag slides towards the outside door.
explanations.art: A top view of a bus turning left, with a girl pressed against the right window, an arrow from the window pointing inward, and a dotted line showing the straight path her body wants.
explanations.context: This card explains the feeling of being pushed outward on a bend.

explanations.concept: A spin sorts things: the dryer, the cream separator and the centrifuge
explanations.definition: In a spinning container, each part needs a pull towards the middle to stay in the circle. Parts that are held go round. Parts that are not held, or are heavier, move to the outside.
explanations.description: In a spin dryer, the wall of the drum holds the clothes in the circle, but the holes in the wall let the water go. Each drop goes straight on and leaves through a hole, so the water leaves and the clothes stay. Milk is a mixture of watery milk and fat, called cream. The watery milk is a little heavier. In a cream separator, the heavier watery milk is pushed to the outside, and the lighter cream gathers nearer the middle. The two leave by different pipes. In a hospital laboratory, a centrifuge spins tubes of blood. The heavier blood cells settle at the bottom of the tube, which is its outer end, and the lighter liquid stays above. Nobody has to choose which part goes where. The spin does it.
examples: A spin dryer throws water out through the holes in the drum, and leaves the clothes behind.
A cream separator spins milk, so that the cream gathers nearer the middle.
A laboratory centrifuge spins blood, so that the heavier blood cells settle at the outer end of the tube.
explanations.art: A spin dryer drum with clothes against the wall and water drops leaving through holes, beside a test tube with settled blood cells at the outer end.
explanations.context: This card is about how spinning separates parts of a mixture.

explanations.concept: Bends in roads, rails and cycles: friction, tilt and lean
explanations.definition: On a flat bend, the friction between the tyres and the road is the pull towards the middle. If the friction is not enough, the vehicle slides straight on. Tilting the road, or leaning the vehicle, helps.
explanations.description: A car on a flat road needs the friction of its tyres to pull it round a bend. On a wet or oily road, there is less friction, so the car can only take the bend at a lower speed. If it goes too fast, it slides straight on, off the road. Road builders tilt bends so that the outside is higher than the inside. Then part of the push of the road points towards the middle, and the car needs less friction. Railways raise the outer rail of a curve for the same reason. A cyclist leans into a bend so that the push of the ground points towards the middle. The faster the speed, or the tighter the bend, the more the cyclist must lean.
examples: A car on a wet road slides straight on if it takes a bend too fast.
On many railway curves the outer rail is a little higher than the inner rail.
A cyclist leans more in a tight turn, and more in a fast turn.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: a car sliding straight off a wet bend, a railway curve with the outer rail higher, and a cyclist leaning into a turn.
explanations.context: This card explains why bends are dangerous at speed, and what builders and riders do about it.

explanations.concept: Circles that go up and down: buckets, loops and giant wheels
explanations.definition: In a circle that goes up and over, the thing must be going fast enough at the top that gravity alone gives all the pull it needs. If it is slower, it leaves the circle and falls.
explanations.description: Swing a bucket of water in a circle over your head. At the top, the water is upside down. It stays in the bucket because the bucket moves down faster than the water would fall. The water presses on the bottom of the bucket, and the bottom pushes back. If you swing too slowly, the water falls out. For a circle with a radius of about 70 centimetres, the slowest safe swing takes about 1.7 seconds for a full turn. In a giant wheel at a mela, you feel lighter at the top, and heavier at the bottom. A roller-coaster train with a loop needs enough speed at the top, so the cars stay on the track. A marble on a loop usually needs to start about 3 times the loop's radius above the bottom of the loop.
examples: Water stays in a bucket swung fast enough in a vertical circle.
A rider on a giant wheel feels lighter at the top and heavier at the bottom.
A marble run with a loop needs the marble to start high enough.
explanations.art: A girl swinging a bucket in a vertical circle, with the bucket at the top upside down and the water staying in it.
explanations.context: This card is about circles that go up and down, such as a swung bucket and a loop.

explanations.concept: The Moon and the satellites: falling and always missing
explanations.definition: The Moon is pulled towards the Earth by gravity. It is also moving sideways. It keeps falling towards the Earth, and keeps missing it, so it goes round.
explanations.description: Newton asked what would happen if a cannon on a very high mountain fired a ball sideways. A slow ball falls to the ground quite near. A faster ball lands further away. A ball fired fast enough keeps falling, but the ground curves away beneath it as fast as it falls, so the ball never lands. The Moon is like that ball. It goes round the Earth once in about 27 days, at about 1 kilometre every second. The International Space Station goes round the Earth about once every 90 minutes, at about 8 kilometres every second. Newton also compared the Moon's fall with the fall of an apple. The Moon is about 60 times as far from the Earth's middle as an apple on the ground. He showed that the pull weakens with the square of the distance, so it is about 3,600 times weaker there. The Moon's sideways speed does the rest.
examples: The Moon goes round the Earth once in about 27 days.
The International Space Station goes round the Earth about once every 90 minutes.
The Earth goes round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second.
explanations.art: A very tall mountain on the Earth with three cannonballs fired at different speeds, the fastest going right round the Earth.
explanations.context: This card applies the same idea to the Moon and to satellites.

explanations.description: Everyone agrees on what happens on a turntable or a bus. Scientists differ on what to call the outward feeling. Many teachers say there is no outward force at all, only inertia and an inward pull. Many engineers, who work inside spinning machines such as centrifuges, use 'centrifugal force' every day because it makes their sums easy. The old argument is about what spinning is measured against. Does a spinning bucket of water show spin in empty space, or only spin compared with the stars? Nobody has settled it.
examples: In a bus on a bend, you are pushed inward by the window, and you press back on it.
Engineers use centrifugal force to design a laboratory centrifuge.

perspectives.explanation: Newton spun a bucket of water and noticed that the water climbs the sides. He argued that this shows real spin, which is not just spin compared with other things.

perspectives.who: Ernst Mach, an Austrian scientist, in 1883
perspectives.explanation: Mach suggested that spin might be spin compared with all the matter in the universe, such as the far stars. Nobody has shown whether he was right.
They teach that there is no outward force. There is the inertia of the thing, which goes straight, and the inward pull. The outward feeling is the push of the inward pull on you.
They use centrifugal force as a handy way to describe what happens inside a spinning machine. It is useful, even if it is not a force in the way a push or a pull is.

explanations.art: A girl in a spinning drum fairground ride pressed against the wall, with two thought bubbles beside her, one saying 'inertia' and one saying 'centrifugal force'.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still discuss: whether the outward feeling should be called a force.

agreed.text: A thing moving in a circle needs a force pointing towards the middle of the circle, all the time.
agreed.evidence: A bag whirled on a string stays in its circle only while the string pulls it in. A car stays on a bend only while the tyres grip. Satellites stay in orbit only because of gravity.

agreed.text: When that force stops, the thing moves off in a straight line along the way it was moving at that moment.
agreed.evidence: Sparks from a grinding wheel, mud from a tyre, drops from a wet umbrella and a released hammer in an athletics match all leave in straight lines.

agreed.text: The force needed equals the mass times the speed times the speed, divided by the radius of the circle.
agreed.evidence: This follows from Newton's second law and has been tested with whirlers like yours, with centrifuges and with satellites, for more than 300 years.

agreed.text: The Moon and satellites are held in orbit by gravity. They keep falling towards the Earth, and keep missing it.
agreed.evidence: The path of the Moon, the International Space Station and the satellites launched by ISRO can all be worked out from gravity and from their sideways speed.

agreed.text: Spinning a mixture moves its heavier parts to the outside and its lighter parts nearer the middle.
agreed.evidence: Dairies use cream separators, and hospital laboratories use centrifuges to separate the cells in blood from the liquid. Both work every day.

agreed.text: On a flat bend, the friction of the tyres supplies the pull. If the friction is not enough, the car slides straight on.
agreed.evidence: Skid marks on wet road bends run in straight lines off the curve. Roads and railways are tilted at bends to help.

challenging.claim: A whirled stone, when let go, flies outward away from the middle.
challenging.who: A common guess among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: While you whirl a stone, you feel it pulling outward on your hand.
challenging.against: When you let go, the stone goes straight along the way it was moving, along the tangent, and not outward along the string. What you felt was the stone's inertia pulling on the string, not a push outward on the stone.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common guess on what happens when you let go.

challenging.claim: Something must push a thing forward all the time to keep it going round.
challenging.who: A common idea among children, and an old idea from teachers who followed Aristotle
challenging.for: A cycle slows down when you stop pedalling, so it feels as if pushing is needed to keep going.
challenging.against: The force that makes a thing go round points towards the middle, at a right angle to its motion. It changes the direction but not the speed. A thing going round on smooth ice needs no forward push, only the pull inward.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that circular motion needs a forward push.

challenging.claim: A heavier coin on a turntable slides off before a lighter one.
challenging.who: A very common guess, because heavier things seem harder to hold
challenging.for: A heavier coin needs a bigger pull to be turned in a circle.
challenging.against: A heavier coin also presses harder on the turntable, so the friction that holds it grows in the same proportion. The two cancel. A heavy coin and a light coin at the same distance slide off at the same speed. Only the distance from the middle, and the roughness of the surface, matter.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess on which coin slides off first.

challenging.claim: The Moon does not fall, because the Earth's gravity does not reach that far.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and adults
challenging.for: The Moon is far from the Earth, and astronauts seem to float up there.
challenging.against: Gravity does reach the Moon. If it did not, the Moon would fly off in a straight line. At the Moon's distance, the Earth's pull is about 3,600 times weaker than here, but it is still enough to bend the Moon's path into a ring. Astronauts float because they are falling together with their spacecraft, not because gravity is missing.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that there is no gravity in space.

challenging.claim: A big spinning space station could give its crew a feeling like gravity.
challenging.who: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a Russian scientist, in the early 1900s, and many engineers since
challenging.for: On a spinning ring, the floor pushes the crew inward, as the wall pushes the clothes in a dryer. The push feels the same as weight.
challenging.against: Nobody has built a large spinning station yet. If it is small, the floor would move faster at the head than at the feet, and people could feel dizzy. A big ring turning slowly works much better.
challenging.context: This card is about making a feeling like gravity by spinning.

challenging.claim: Centrifugal force is a real outward force, like a push or a pull.
challenging.for: Inside a spinning machine, everything behaves as if it were pushed outward, and it is easy to calculate with.
challenging.against: Seen from outside, there is no outward force. There is only inertia, and the inward pull. Many physicists call it a helpful pretend force that only appears when you are inside the spin.
challenging.context: This card is about a name that scientists and engineers use differently.

big_questions.q: On a bus bend, you feel pushed outward, yet nobody is pushing you. Where does the feeling come from, and is the push real?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your body is doing, what the window is doing, and whether a feeling needs a push from outside.

big_questions.q: The Moon is falling towards the Earth all the time, yet it never gets closer. How can something fall and never arrive?
big_questions.hint: Think of a ball fired sideways from a very high mountain, faster and faster.

big_questions.q: If you were in a closed room with no windows, how could you tell whether the room was sitting on the ground in gravity, or spinning in space?
big_questions.hint: Think of the clothes pressed against the wall of the dryer. What would a ball do if you dropped it?

big_questions.q: If you whirl a bag twice as fast, the pull is four times as big. Why would nature make the pull grow faster than the speed?
big_questions.hint: Think of two things happening at once when you go twice as fast in the same circle.

big_questions.q: Many things in the sky go round: the Moon, the Earth, whole galaxies. Why do almost all of them spin?
big_questions.hint: Think of a big cloud of gas that shrinks and begins to turn. What happens to a turn when something gets smaller?

big_questions.q: Would you like to live in a spinning space town? What would 'down' mean there, and what would be strange?
big_questions.hint: Think of the floor of a giant wheel, and what happens if you walk along it or throw a ball.

big_questions.q: Who decides how fast a car may take a bend, and how do they know it is safe for every driver?
big_questions.hint: Think of a road builder, a wet day, a heavy lorry and an old tyre.

big_questions.q: A spin separates milk from cream and blood cells from liquid without anyone choosing what goes where. What other sorting happens in nature without a sorter?
big_questions.hint: Think of heavy pebbles and light sand in a river, or the layers of oil on water.

story.title: The Wheel That Threw Its Clay
story.note: Thulasi, Kamatchi Paati, Mani Anna, Bala and this morning are made up. Manamadurai, near Madurai, is a real town known for its clay pots, and Karthigai Deepam is a real festival of lamps in Tamil Nadu. The science in the story is real: potters slow the wheel for wide pots, and wet clay leaves a wheel that spins too fast in straight lines.
text: In Manamadurai, a town known for its clay pots, every morning began with the smell of wet earth. Thulasi was ten. She sat beside her grandmother, Kamatchi Paati, at the old wooden wheel in the courtyard, and watched her hands.

Paati's wheel was a heavy stone disc on a pin. She turned it with a stick, and it hummed round and round. On top of it sat a ball of wet clay. With two wet thumbs, Paati opened the ball like a flower. In a minute, it was a pot.

Before Karthigai Deepam, the festival of lamps, the whole street made diyas. This year, a shop in Madurai had asked for five hundred, and the temple had asked for forty wide water bowls. Paati's arms were tired. Her eyes were tired too.

On Monday, a man called Mani Anna came with a box and a motor. He fitted a belt to the wheel and plugged it in. 'Now it turns by itself,' he said. 'Faster than any stick. Turn the knob to the right, and it goes quicker, and quicker still. You will finish your order in half the time.'
Thulasi's little brother Bala clapped. Paati looked at the knob with narrow eyes. 'A wheel is a friend,' she said slowly. 'But a friend who is asked to go too fast will let go of you.'

Mani Anna laughed. He turned the knob all the way to the right. The disc hummed. Paati put a ball of clay in the middle and opened it with her thumbs. At once the clay began to climb up and out. Then flick, flick, flick, lumps of clay and drops of water flew off the wheel. They spattered across the wall, and across Bala's face. The pot sagged and tore.
'Aiyo!' said Bala. Mani Anna wiped his cheek. 'Maybe too fast,' he said. 'But what is the right speed?'

Nobody answered. Thulasi looked at the wall. The spots on it were not in a ring round the wheel. They were in long, straight streaks, like arrows. Each streak began at the edge of the wheel and pointed along the way the wheel had been turning.
'Paati,' she said. 'The drops did not fly outward. They flew straight on.' 'Go on,' said Paati.

'The clay at the edge goes round and round,' said Thulasi. 'Something must hold it in. The wet clay holds on to the wheel, and holds on to the clay beside it. When the wheel is slow, the holding is enough. When the wheel is fast, the holding is not enough. Then the drop is let go, and it goes straight, the way it was already moving.'
Mani Anna scratched his head. 'But how fast is too fast?'
'It depends where you are,' said Thulasi. 'Clay near the middle goes round a tiny circle. Clay at the edge goes round a big one, and moves much faster. So the edge lets go first.'

She dipped her finger in water and put a drop near the middle of the disc. Then she put another near the edge. 'Turn it very slowly, Anna,' she said. He turned the knob one notch. Both drops stayed. Two notches, and the drop at the edge rolled off. The drop in the middle stayed until the fourth notch.

'The wider the pot, the closer the clay is to the edge,' said Paati softly. 'My mother told me, the wider the pot, the slower the wheel. I have known it in my hands for sixty years. Now this girl knows it in words.'

They tried again. For the narrow diyas, Mani Anna turned the knob to the fourth notch. For the wide water bowls, only to the second. The clay stayed on the wheel. The pots rose smooth and round, one after another, like lotus buds.

When the order was done, Mani Anna painted four little marks on the knob, and wrote 'Thulasi's rule' beside them. 'Wide pot, slow wheel,' he said. 'Narrow pot, quicker wheel.' Thulasi looked at the wall, where the streaks of clay still pointed along the way the wheel had turned. The clay had never wanted to go round, she thought. It only wanted to go straight, and the wheel had kept asking it to turn.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a circle needs a pull towards the middle at every moment, and in the wheel that pull is the grip of the wet clay. The pull needed grows with the square of the speed, and with the distance from the middle, so the edge of the wheel is the first place where the grip fails. When the grip fails, the clay does not move outward. It goes straight, along the way it was moving, which is why the streaks on the wall were straight. Wide pots reach out to the edge, so they need a slower wheel. This is the same rule as the whirler and the coins on the turntable.
ask: Why were the streaks on the wall straight, and not curved?
Why did the drop at the edge of the wheel roll off before the drop near the middle?
Why does a wide pot need a slower wheel than a narrow one?
Thulasi tested with drops of water before she told anyone her idea. Why might that have been better than just saying it?
How could you test Thulasi's rule with a turntable and some coins?

roots.context: We have measured the pull that keeps a bag going round, and seen what happens when it stops. Now we ask what going round tells us about the world and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: The bag on your string was pulled inward the whole time, yet it never came closer. It kept moving sideways while it was pulled. So going round is falling inward and sideways together, without ever arriving. The Moon moves like this round the Earth.
deep_truth.habit: We treat falling and going round as opposites. A fall ends on the ground, and going round seems calm and steady. But a thing in a circle is pulled inward every moment, and never arrives only because its sideways motion keeps carrying it past.
deep_truth.evidence: In the whirler test, the bag kept circling only while the coins pulled on the string, and a faster circle needed many more coins. Without that pull, things leave in straight lines. If your results differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: You are riding on a spinning Earth, and the Earth is going round the Sun. Gravity holds you to the ground while you are carried round, and you feel nothing of it.
three.what_is_life: A crow turning in the air tilts her body into the turn, and a girl on a cycle leans into the bend. Living bodies learn how much to lean for the speed and the circle.
three.what_is_this_world: A stone on a string, wet clothes in a dryer and the Moon going round the Earth all follow one rule. A thing goes round only while something pulls it towards the middle.

roots.thread: Look at the stone on the string, the clothes in the dryer and the Moon together. Each is pulled towards a middle, and each would go straight on if the pull stopped. The circle is what you get when those two meet. The same simple rule holds from a toy to a planet: the pull needed grows with the square of the speed. So the many circles of the world come from one pull and one straight-line habit.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet in one hub, but it is the empty space in the hub that makes the wheel useful.
teachings.link: At the middle of the whirler there is only a hole in a pen. Yet the pull on the bag points to it all the time. The empty middle holds everything in its circle.

teachings.teaching: The ancient singers of the Rig Veda spoke of a wheel with twelve spokes that turns round the sky and does not wear out. They saw the turning of the sky as a wheel of order.
teachings.link: Today we know that a pull towards a middle keeps the Moon and the planets going round, year after year, just like the bag on a string.

science.text: A thing in a circle needs a force towards the middle that equals its mass times its speed times its speed, divided by the radius. This holds from whirled bags to planets.
Whether the outward feeling on a bend should be called a force, and what spin is measured against, are still discussed by physicists and philosophers.

other_view.who: Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity
other_view.view: In Einstein's theory, nothing pulls the Moon at all. The Earth bends space and time around it, and the Moon follows the straightest path through that bent space. 'Falling' is then another way to describe the same thing, and 'a pull' is a picture that works very well but is not the last word.

practice.title: The slow turn
practice.say: Stand with your arms hanging loose. Turn slowly on the spot, once all the way round. Notice that your arms drift outward a little. Now stand still, and breathe out slowly three times. Feel the floor pushing up on your feet. Remember that the Earth is turning, and you are riding it.
practice.kid: Stand up. Let your arms hang loose. Turn slowly once. Feel your arms drift out. Now stand still. Breathe out slowly three times.

ask: If going round is falling sideways, what are you falling around right now?
Is the feeling of being pushed outward on a bend real, if nobody is pushing you?
Is a pull a thing in the world, or a picture we draw to describe how things move?

games.title: Where Does It Go Next?
games.context: This is a card game about things that go round. Each card describes a moment. You decide what happens next, and say why.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a moment on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A stone is whirled in a circle on a string. The string snaps.
items.b: Flies off straight. With no pull towards the middle, the stone goes along the way it was moving at that moment.

items.f: A stone is whirled on a string. The thrower doubles the speed in the same circle. What does the string need?
items.b: Bigger pull needed. Twice the speed needs four times the pull.

items.f: A stone is whirled at a steady speed. The string is made twice as long, so the circle is twice as wide, and the speed stays the same. What does the string need?
items.b: Smaller pull needed. A wider circle at the same speed needs half the pull.

items.f: The Moon moves sideways, and the Earth's gravity pulls it all the time.
items.b: Keeps going round. The Moon keeps falling towards the Earth and keeps missing it.

items.f: A car is taking a bend at 20 kilometres an hour. The driver slows to 10. What happens to the grip the tyres need?
items.b: Smaller pull needed. Half the speed needs only one quarter of the grip.

items.f: A car takes a bend on a wet road, going so fast that the tyres cannot grip.
items.b: Flies off straight. The car slides straight on, along the way it was moving.

items.f: A piece of mud is stuck to a fast-turning bicycle tyre, and it comes loose.
items.b: Flies off straight. The mud goes along the way the tyre was moving at that moment.

items.f: A grinding wheel throws off sparks.
items.b: Flies off straight. Each spark leaves along a straight line that just touches the wheel.

items.f: A wet umbrella is spun round by its handle. What do the drops of water do?
items.b: Flies off straight. Each drop leaves along the way it was moving.

items.f: A marble goes round inside a kadai at a steady speed, with the kadai wall pushing it inward.
items.b: Keeps going round. The wall gives the pull towards the middle.

items.f: A heavy stone and a light stone are whirled at the same speed in circles of the same size. What does the string of the heavy stone need?
items.b: Bigger pull needed. A bigger mass needs a bigger pull.

items.f: Wet clothes spin in a dryer drum with holes in its wall. What do the drops of water do when they reach a hole?
items.b: Flies off straight. The hole lets the drop go, and it carries on in a straight line.

items.f: The clothes in the same dryer. What does the drum wall do to them?
items.b: Keeps going round. The wall pushes the clothes inward and holds them in the circle.

items.f: A child sits on a merry-go-round near the middle, then moves to the edge. The merry-go-round turns at the same rate. What does the child need?
items.b: Bigger pull needed. At the edge, the child goes round a bigger circle and moves faster.

items.f: A satellite is going round the Earth. Imagine that the Earth's pull suddenly vanished.
items.b: Flies off straight. With no pull, the satellite goes straight on, along the way it was moving.

items.f: A cyclist goes round a bend at a steady speed, leaning inward.
items.b: Keeps going round. The push of the ground, through the leaning cycle, points towards the middle.

items.f: The cyclist goes through the same bend, but faster. What does the cyclist need?
items.b: Bigger pull needed. A faster speed needs a much bigger pull, so the cyclist must lean more.

items.f: The bend is made wider, and the cyclist keeps the same speed. What does the cyclist need?
items.b: Smaller pull needed. A wider circle at the same speed needs less pull.

items.f: A coin sits at the edge of a turntable. The turntable spins faster than the friction can hold.
items.b: Flies off straight. The coin slides off along a straight line.

items.f: The same coin is moved halfway to the middle of the turntable, with the turntable turning at the same rate. What does the coin need?
items.b: Smaller pull needed. Nearer the middle, the circle is smaller and the coin moves more slowly.

items.f: A hammer thrower in an athletics match lets go of the hammer's handle.
items.b: Flies off straight. The hammer goes along the way it was moving when let go, so the thrower lets go at the right moment.

items.f: A roller-coaster car, moving fast enough, goes up and over a loop.
items.b: Keeps going round. The track pushes the car, and gravity helps at the top.

items.f: A heavy lorry and a car take the same bend at the same speed. What do the lorry's tyres need?
items.b: Bigger pull needed. The lorry has more mass, so its tyres must give more grip.

items.f: A bucket of water is swung fast in a circle over someone's head. What does the water do at the top?
items.b: Keeps going round. The bucket moves down faster than the water would fall, so the water stays in.

printables.title: 8 tokens: two sets of four, which say Flies off straight, Keeps going round, Bigger pull needed and Smaller pull needed

setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A boy reading a card aloud, while two other players each push a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone picks a token and puts it face down.

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every card is about what happens next, or what the pull towards the middle must be.
Every other player picks one token: Flies off straight, Keeps going round, Bigger pull needed, or Smaller pull needed.
Everyone puts the token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. Each right token scores 1 point. A player who also gives the right reason scores 1 more.
Take turns as the reader. A game is 12 cards. If there is time, shuffle and play 12 more.
The player with the most points wins, and ties share the win. Playing alone? Read the front, pick a token, then check the back. Try to beat your last score out of 12.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes a moment. You pick a token to show what happens next. Each player takes four tokens.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take your four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does It Go Next. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. A stone is whirled on a string, and the string snaps. Everyone picks a token and turns it over together.
flow.say: Practice card. A stone is whirled in a circle on a string, and the string snaps. Pick a token, then turn it over.
flow.kid: Practice card. The string snaps. Pick a token. Turn it over.

check.q: A stone is whirled in a circle on a string, and the string snaps. What does the stone do?
options: Flies off straight, along the way it was moving
Flies outward, away from the middle
Keeps going round in a circle
check.why: When the pull stops, nothing bends the path of the stone. It goes straight on, along the way it was moving at that moment. Picking 'outward' mixes up what the string feels with what the stone does. Picking 'round' forgets that the string was the thing holding it in the circle.

flow.context: In this step, you play one practice card to learn how the game works.

flow.do: Take turns as the reader. Play the first 6 cards. After each card, ask who can say why.
flow.say: Reader, read the front. Everyone picks a token. Turn them over together. Now read the back. Who can say why?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the 'Flies off straight' cards have in common?
good: The pull towards the middle stopped or was not enough.
The thing went along the way it was already moving.
Nothing was bending its path any more.

flow.parent: Give 1 bonus point for a reason that uses the pull towards the middle, the speed, the radius or the mass. A guess such as 'it flies out' needs a follow-up: out along the string, or straight on along the way it was moving?
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next 6 cards. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Keep going. Read, pick, turn over and check. Which cards made you change your mind?
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Which card made you change your mind?

ask.q: Look at the cards where the answer was 'Bigger pull needed'. What do they have in common?
good: The speed went up, or the mass went up.
The thing moved faster or went round a bigger circle at the same rate.
More mass or more speed means more pull.

flow.parent: The 'Smaller pull needed' cards are about a wider circle or a slower speed. The 'Bigger pull needed' cards are about a faster speed, a bigger mass or a position nearer the edge. Remember that doubling the speed needs four times the pull.
flow.context: In this step, you play more cards and look for a pattern in the answers.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which card was the hardest, and why.
flow.say: Add up your points. Which card was the hardest? What would you check next time?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which card was the hardest? Why?

check.q: A car goes through a bend at 30 kilometres an hour. Then it goes through the same bend at 60 kilometres an hour. How does the grip it needs change?
options: It needs four times as much grip
It needs twice as much grip
It needs the same grip
check.why: Twice the speed in the same bend needs four times the pull towards the middle. Picking 'twice as much' forgets that a faster car both turns more quickly and has more speed to turn. The two effects multiply.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the scores and try one last tricky card.

experiments.title: The Whirler: how fast must a bag go round for each size of pull?
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. A small bag whirls round on a string through a pen, while coins hang from the other end. You count how many turns the bag makes for each size of pull.
experiments.question: A small bag whirls in a circle on a string, and the pull on the string comes from coins hanging at the other end. When the pull is bigger, how much faster must the bag go round to stay in the same circle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you use four times as many coins, will the bag need to go round four times as fast, or less than four times as fast, or more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bag, the same string, the same pen, and the same length of string from the pen to the bag every time. A piece of tape on the string marks the length. Only the number of coins at the hanging end changes: 4, 8, then 16. Keep the tape at the top of the pen while you whirl. The helper counts how many turns the bag makes in 10 seconds. Do 3 tries for each number of coins, because one try can be a fluke, and use the middle result.

materials.item: a plastic ball-pen barrel about 12 centimetres long, with the ink refill taken out by a grown-up and the ends smooth
a strong thin string or thread about 1.5 metres long
a very light soft bag: a small cloth or handkerchief tied round 2 one-rupee coins
a small pouch tied to the other end of the string, and 16 one-rupee coins to put in it
a piece of coloured tape and a ruler or measuring tape
a phone or watch with a stopwatch, and a helper to time and count the turns
a clear space about 3 metres across, away from people, glass, fans and tube lights, such as a hall or a terrace

schedule.what: Guess. Build the whirler. Practise. Count the turns for 4, 8 and 16 coins. Say what you found.

experiments.safety: Use only the soft bag, never a hard object. Whirl it in front of you at arm's length, away from faces and from other people. A grown-up stays close. Keep coins away from children under five.
experiments.record: Fill in the table, one row for each number of coins. Then draw a bar chart of the middle results. Under the chart, write how the turns changed when the coins became four times as many.

setup.art: A plastic pen barrel with a string running through it, a small cloth bag tied to the top end and a pouch of coins tied to the bottom end.
setup.caption: 1. Thread the string through the pen. Tie the bag to the top and the pouch to the bottom.

setup.art: A piece of coloured tape stuck on the string 50 centimetres from the bag, with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stick tape on the string 50 centimetres from the bag.

setup.art: Four one-rupee coins being put into a small pouch hanging below the pen.
setup.caption: 3. Put 4 coins in the pouch.

setup.art: A girl holding the pen upright at arm's length and whirling the small bag in a circle in front of her, while a boy watches with a stopwatch and the pouch hangs still below the pen.
setup.caption: 4. Whirl the bag. Keep the tape at the top of the pen.

setup.art: A notebook with a table of turns and a bar chart with three bars drawn under it.
setup.caption: 5. Write the results in the table. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: Show your child the pen, the string, the bag and the pouch of coins. Explain that the coins pull the string, and the bag must go round fast enough to hold the string still. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The coins hang below and pull on the string. The bag must go round fast enough to hold them up. If we use four times as many coins, how much faster must the bag go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Coins pull the string. The bag goes round to hold them. Four times the coins. How much faster must the bag go? Why?

ask.q: If the coins are four times as many, how many times as fast must the bag go round? Why?
good: Four times as fast, because the pull is four times as big.
Less than four times as fast.
Twice as fast.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say four times as fast. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Whirler test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up takes the ink refill out of the pen and checks the ends are smooth. 2. Push the string through the pen. 3. Tie the bag to one end. 4. Tie the pouch to the other end. 5. Stick the tape on the string 50 centimetres from the bag. 6. Put 4 coins in the pouch.
flow.say: We are building the whirler. The string goes through the pen. The bag is on top and the coins hang below. The tape shows how long the string is above the pen.
flow.kid: Thread the string through the pen. Tie on the bag. Tie on the pouch. Stick on the tape.
flow.parent: The bag should be as light as you can make it, just 2 coins in a knotted handkerchief. If the pouch is lighter than the bag, the bag will hang down instead of whirling. Check that no sharp edge of the pen can rub the string.

check.q: Why is a piece of tape stuck on the string at 50 centimetres from the bag?
options: So the circle is the same size every time
So the string looks neat
So the coins stay in the pouch
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the string above the pen were longer at times, the circle would be bigger, and a longer time could be because of the bigger circle and not because of the coins.

flow.context: In this step, you build the whirler. The pen, the string and the bag are the same for every test.

flow.do: Hold the pen upright at arm's length, in front of you. Whirl the bag in a circle. Find the speed at which the pouch stays still and the tape stays at the top of the pen. Practise until you can keep it steady for 10 seconds.
flow.say: Whirl the bag. If the pouch drops, whirl a little faster. If the pouch rises, slow down a little. Find the speed that keeps the tape still.
flow.kid: Whirl the bag. Pouch drops? Go faster. Pouch rises? Go slower. Keep the tape still.
flow.parent: A grown-up stands close. If the bag will not whirl and hangs low, add 2 coins to the pouch or use a lighter bag. It takes most children a few tries. The speed does not need to be exact. A small band of speeds keeps the tape steady, so aim for the middle of it.
flow.context: In this step, you practise whirling the bag at the speed that holds the coins up.

flow.do: Put 4 coins in the pouch. Whirl the bag steadily. The helper starts the stopwatch and counts the turns in 10 seconds. Do 3 tries. Then repeat with 8 coins, then with 16 coins.
flow.say: Start whirling. When the tape is steady, say go. Count every time the bag passes in front of you for 10 seconds. Write down the number.
flow.kid: Whirl the bag steadily. The helper counts the turns in 10 seconds. Do it three times for each pouch.
flow.parent: Use the middle of the three results. With more coins, the bag should go round faster and faster. With 16 coins the bag goes round nearly twice every second, so the helper can count in twos or film it. Expect roughly 9, 13 and 18 turns for 4, 8 and 16 coins. Four times the coins should need about twice the turns, not four times. If counting is hard, film the bag with a phone and count the turns when you play it back.

check.q: With 16 coins, the bag went round faster than with 4 coins. Why did it need to?
options: A bigger pull on the string needs a faster circle to match it
The bigger pouch made the string shorter
A faster bag is always lighter
check.why: The coins pull the bag inward. To go round in the same circle, the bag needs a pull towards the middle that equals the coins' pull. A bigger pull goes with a faster speed. The tape shows that the string did not get shorter, and the bag did not get lighter.

flow.context: In this step, you change only the number of coins, and count the turns for each.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: their claim, their evidence and their reason. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what numbers show it. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: When the coins became four times as many, how many times as many turns did the bag need?
good: About twice as many turns.
Less than four times as many.
The turns grew more slowly than the coins.

flow.think: The pouch of coins is the thing that pulled the bag inward. If the string snapped, where would the bag go?
flow.parent: After your child has said their ideas, tell them: this fits the rule. Twice the speed needs four times the pull. Four times the coins needed only about twice the turns. If the results were messy, say that scientists see that too, and that is why we do each setting three times.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, how you know, and why you think it happened.

experiments.title: Coins on the Turntable: which one slides off first?
experiments.context: In this experiment, coins sit on a plate that you turn faster and faster. You find out which coin slides off first, and whether a heavy coin slides off before a light one.
experiments.question: Coins sit at different distances from the middle of a plate that turns faster and faster. Which coin slides off first? Does a heavy stack of coins slide off before a single coin?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which coin will slide off first, the one near the middle or the one near the edge? Will a heavy stack of coins slide off before a single coin? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same plate and the same type of coin every time. In Part A, put three coins on rings marked at 5, 10 and 15 centimetres from the middle, on different sides of the plate. Turn the plate faster in steps: one turn in 4 seconds, in 3 seconds, in 2 seconds, and then as fast as you safely can. In Part B, put a single coin and a stack of 3 coins taped together on the same ring, on opposite sides. Do 3 tries of each part, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a turntable you can turn by hand, such as a swivel stool or chair seat, a lazy Susan, a revolving cake stand, or an upside-down cycle with a cardboard disc fixed on its wheel
a smooth flat steel plate (thali) or plastic tray about 25 centimetres across, to put on the turntable
6 one-rupee coins, and a little tape to join 3 of them into a stack
a marker or chalk, and a ruler, to draw rings 5, 10 and 15 centimetres from the middle
a helper to turn the turntable and count aloud

schedule.what: Guess. Draw the rings. Turn the plate faster and faster with three coins on it. Try a stack and a single coin on the same ring. Say what you found.

experiments.safety: Nobody sits on the turntable. Keep fingers away from the moving seat, and turn it by hand only. Stand a metre back, because a coin can fly off. Keep coins away from children under five.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for each try. Draw a picture of the plate from above, with the three coins on their rings, and number them in the order that they slid off.

setup.art: A boy turning a swivel stool seat by hand with the plate on it, while a girl counts aloud, standing a metre back.

setup.caption: 3. Turn faster and faster. Which coin slides off first?
