flow.do: Show your child the plate, the coins and the turntable. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guesses on a sheet of paper.
flow.say: We will put coins on a plate and turn it faster and faster. Which coin do you think will slide off first? Will a heavy stack slide off before a single coin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Coins on a plate that turns faster and faster. Which slides off first? Will a heavy stack go before one coin? Why?

ask.q: Which coin do you think will slide off first, and why?
good: The one near the edge, because it goes round a bigger circle.
The one near the middle.
The heavy one, because it is harder to hold.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say a heavy stack will slide off first. Write down what your child says and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coins on the Turntable test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Draw three rings on the plate, at 5, 10 and 15 centimetres from the middle. 2. Put the plate on the turntable, with its middle over the middle of the turntable. 3. Put one coin on each ring, on different sides of the plate. 4. Tape three coins into a stack.
flow.say: We will draw three rings on the plate. The coins will sit on different rings and on different sides, so they do not bump each other.
flow.kid: Draw three rings on the plate. Put one coin on each ring, on different sides.
flow.parent: The plate must be flat and centred on the turntable. The smoother the plate, the easier it is for a coin to slide. If your plate is rough, put a sheet of smooth plastic on it. Wipe the coins and the plate clean first.

check.q: Why do we put the coins on different sides of the plate, and not in a line?
options: So that a coin that slides off does not knock the others
So that the plate looks neat
So that the heavy coin is on the left
check.why: A coin that slides off in a line would crash into the coin beyond it, and spoil the test. Putting the coins on different sides keeps each coin's path clear.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the plate and the coins.

flow.do: Part A. The helper turns the plate by hand. First one turn in 4 seconds, counting 'one-and, two-and, three-and, four-and'. Then one turn in 3 seconds, then in 2 seconds, then as fast as is safe. After each speed, stop and look at which coins are left. Do 3 tries.
flow.say: Turn the plate slowly, one turn for each count of four. Keep it steady for three turns. Then go a little faster. Stop each time and look. Which coin has gone?
flow.kid: Turn the plate slowly. Keep it steady. Then go faster. Stop and look. Which coin has gone?
flow.parent: On a smooth steel plate, the coin at 15 centimetres usually slides when a turn takes about 1.5 to 2 seconds. The coin at 10 centimetres goes at a quicker turn, and the coin at 5 centimetres may only go at about one turn a second, which may be as fast as a hand can turn it. If nothing slides, use a smoother plate. If all of the coins slide at the slowest speed, use a rougher plate. Write down the order each time.

check.q: The coin at the edge of the plate slid off before the coin near the middle. What is the best reason?
options: The coin at the edge goes round a bigger circle, and needs more friction to stay on
The coin at the edge is heavier
The coin near the middle is stuck to the plate
check.why: The edge coin goes round a bigger circle and moves faster, so it needs a bigger pull towards the middle. Friction is the only pull the plate gives, so the edge coin loses its grip first. The coins had the same weight, and none was stuck.

flow.context: In this step, you turn the plate faster and faster, and see which coin slides off first.

flow.do: Part B. Take the coins off. Put a single coin and the stack of 3 coins on opposite sides of the 10 centimetre ring. Turn the plate faster and faster as before. Watch which one slides first. Do 3 tries.
flow.say: Now a single coin and a heavy stack sit on the same ring. Which will slide off first? Turn the plate faster, and watch.
flow.kid: A single coin and a stack on the same ring. Turn faster. Which slides first?
flow.parent: The stack and the single coin should slide off at about the same time. If the stack slides a little before or after, the tape or the plate may be uneven, so repeat the try. The stack is three times as heavy, so it needs three times the pull. It also presses three times as hard on the plate, so the friction is three times as big.

check.q: The single coin and the stack of three coins slid off at about the same time. What is the best explanation?
options: The stack needs three times the pull, but the plate also grips it three times as hard
The stack has no weight
Coins never slide off in stacks
check.why: A heavier stack needs a bigger pull to go round, because it has more mass. It also presses harder on the plate, so the friction that holds it grows in the same proportion. The two cancel, so the stack and the single coin slide off at the same speed.

flow.context: In this step, you test whether a heavy stack of coins slides off before a single coin.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write their claim, their evidence and their reason. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you find? Which coin went first? Did the heavy stack go first? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why did the coin at the edge go first, and why did the stack and the single coin go together?
good: The edge goes round a bigger circle, so it needs more friction.
The stack is heavier, but it also grips harder.
Only the distance from the middle and the plate mattered.

flow.think: The friction of the plate was the only pull towards the middle. What would happen with a rougher plate?
flow.parent: After your child has said their ideas: friction is the pull towards the middle. A coin slides off when the speed is too high for the friction to hold it. The pull needed grows with the distance from the middle and with the square of the speed. The friction available grows with the weight, and so does the pull needed. So the weight cancels, and only the distance and the roughness are left.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, how you know, and why you think it happened.

activities.title: Feel the Pull: three little tests with one sock
activities.context: In this short activity, you whirl a soft sock on a string and feel the pull on your fingers. You find out what makes the pull bigger.

materials.item: a long shoelace or string about 1 metre long
a soft rolled sock, tied to one end of the string
5 one-rupee coins, to put inside the sock for the heavier test
a clear space about 3 metres across, away from people and breakable things

schedule.what: Guess. Whirl the sock slowly and then faster. Whirl a heavier sock. Say what changed in your fingers.

activities.safety: Whirl only a soft sock, in a flat circle at about waist height, away from faces and from other people. A grown-up stays close. Keep coins away from children under five.
activities.record: Draw the sock going round, with an arrow along the string showing the pull. Draw a long arrow for the strong pull and a short arrow for the weak pull.

setup.art: A girl holding the end of a string between her finger and thumb and whirling a rolled sock slowly in a flat circle at waist height.
setup.caption: 1. Whirl the sock slowly. Feel the pull on your fingers.

setup.art: The same girl whirling the sock faster, with the string stretched straight and a longer arrow along it.
setup.caption: 2. Whirl it faster. Is the pull bigger?

setup.art: The girl whirling a heavier sock with coins inside, at the same speed as the first.
setup.caption: 3. Put coins in the sock. Whirl it at the same speed.

flow.do: Show the sock on its string. Ask your child to guess how the pull on their fingers will change. Try a faster sock and a heavier sock. Ask why.
flow.say: I will whirl the sock slowly, then faster. Then I will put coins in it. What do you think will happen to the pull on your fingers? Why?
flow.kid: Whirl the sock slowly, then fast, then with coins. How will the pull feel? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the pull when you whirl faster?
good: It will pull harder.
It will pull about twice as hard.
I am not sure.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Pull. You guess before you whirl.

flow.do: Hold the end of the string between finger and thumb. Whirl the sock slowly in a flat circle at waist height. Feel the pull. Then whirl it twice as fast. Feel the pull again.
flow.say: Whirl the sock slowly. Feel the string pulling your fingers. Now go faster. Is the pull bigger or smaller? How much bigger?
flow.kid: Whirl the sock slowly. Feel the pull. Now whirl it faster. Feel the pull again.
flow.parent: Keep the circle flat and at waist height. Stand well away from other people. A grown-up should be close. The pull at twice the speed should feel much more than twice as strong.

check.q: You whirled the sock twice as fast and the pull on your fingers got much stronger. What is the best explanation?
options: A faster circle needs a much bigger pull towards the middle
A faster sock gets heavier
The string gets shorter when you whirl
check.why: The string pulls the sock towards your fingers, and the sock pulls back on the string by the same amount. Going twice as fast needs four times the pull. The sock's mass and the string's length did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you whirl the sock slowly and then faster, and feel the pull.

flow.do: Put 5 coins inside the sock and tie it shut. Whirl it at the same speed as the slow whirl. Feel the pull. Is it bigger or smaller than for the plain sock?
flow.say: Now the sock is heavier. Whirl it at the same slow speed as before. Is the pull bigger or smaller?
flow.kid: Put coins in the sock. Whirl it at the same speed. Is the pull bigger or smaller?
flow.parent: Tie the sock tightly, so no coin can fly out. The pull from the heavier sock at the same speed should feel clearly bigger, because a bigger mass needs a bigger pull to be turned.
flow.context: In this step, you whirl a heavier sock at the same speed, and feel the pull.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: Your fingers felt the string pulling outward on them. What was the string doing to the sock?
flow.kid: Your fingers feel a pull. What is the string doing to the sock?

ask.q: The string pulled your fingers outward. In which direction was it pulling the sock?
good: Inward, towards my hand.
To the middle of the circle.
The string pulls both ways, as hard each way.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: the string pulls the sock inward, towards the middle, and the sock pulls the string outward just as hard. Your fingers feel the outward pull of the sock. The pull on the sock itself is the one that makes it go round.
flow.context: In this step, you find out which way the string pulls the sock.

activities.title: Marble in the Kadai: how high will it climb?
activities.context: In this activity, you swirl a marble round inside a kadai and watch it climb up the wall. You find out what makes it climb, and why it spirals down when it slows.

materials.item: a steel kadai or a wide deep bowl
a marble (goli) or a small steel ball
a firm table or a clear floor, with a towel under the kadai to quieten the noise

schedule.what: Guess. Swirl the marble gently and then harder. Watch how high it climbs. Let it slow down and watch how it spirals in.

activities.safety: Keep the marble away from children under five, who might put it in their mouths. Do this over a table or the floor, not on a high shelf.
activities.record: Draw the kadai from above and from the side. Draw the path of the marble when you swirl gently and when you swirl hard.

setup.art: A girl holding a steel kadai by its two handles over a towel on a table, with a marble resting in the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the kadai. Put the marble in the bottom.

setup.art: The kadai being moved in small circles, with the marble going round low on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Move the kadai in small circles. The marble starts going round.

setup.art: The marble going round higher on the wall of the kadai, with a longer arrow showing faster motion.
setup.caption: 3. Swirl harder. Does the marble climb higher?

flow.do: Show the kadai and the marble. Ask your child to guess how high the marble will climb if the kadai is swirled gently, and then harder. Ask why.
flow.say: I will put a marble in this kadai and swirl it. How high up the wall do you think it will go if I swirl it harder? Why?
flow.kid: Swirl the marble in the kadai. Harder swirl, higher marble? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the marble when the swirl gets faster?
good: It will climb higher up the wall.
It will fly out of the kadai.
It will go round faster.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children think the marble will fly out. It stays in, because the wall pushes it inward.
flow.context: This is the first step of Marble in the Kadai. You guess before you swirl.

flow.do: Hold the kadai by its handles over the towel. Move it in small circles with your hands until the marble goes round on the wall. First go round gently, then swirl harder. Watch how high the marble goes each time.
flow.say: Move the kadai in small circles. The marble will start to go round. Now swirl a little harder. How high does the marble go?
flow.kid: Swirl the kadai in small circles. Watch the marble. Swirl harder. How high does it go?
flow.parent: It takes a few tries to start the marble going round. Use small, quick circles with your hands, and do not tilt the kadai. The marble should climb higher the faster it goes. If it jumps out, swirl more gently.

check.q: The marble went round higher on the wall when you swirled faster. What is the best explanation?
options: A faster marble needs a bigger push from the wall towards the middle, and the wall pushes harder higher up
The marble gets lighter when it goes fast
The kadai pulls the marble up
check.why: The wall pushes the marble inward and upward. The steeper part of the wall, higher up, pushes more inward. A faster marble needs a bigger inward push, so it climbs to where the wall can give it. The marble does not get lighter, and the kadai does not pull.

flow.context: In this step, you swirl the marble gently and then harder, and watch how high it climbs.

flow.do: Stop swirling the kadai and hold it still. Watch the marble slow down. Notice how it spirals down towards the bottom, going round more slowly and with a smaller circle each time.
flow.say: Hold the kadai still. Watch the marble. What does its path do as it slows down? Where does it end up?
flow.kid: Hold the kadai still. Watch the marble slow down. What does its path do?
flow.parent: Friction slowly takes away the marble's speed. As it slows, the wall can no longer hold it at that height, so it sinks lower. At the bottom it stops, because there is no wall to push it sideways.
flow.context: In this step, you let the marble slow down and watch its path.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: While the marble went round, it seemed to press on the wall as if it wanted to go outward. What was really pushing it inward?
flow.kid: The marble seems to push outward on the wall. What is pushing it inward?

ask.q: The marble pressed on the wall. What was pushing the marble inward?
good: The wall of the kadai.
The wall pushes back on it.
The kadai gives the pull to the middle.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: the marble presses on the wall because it tries to go straight on. The wall pushes back inward, and that push is what bends the marble's path into a circle. The push on the marble is inward, and the press on the wall is the marble's own pressing.
flow.context: In this step, you find out what pushes the marble inward.

activities.title: Water Stays Up: the slowest swing that keeps the water in
activities.context: In this activity, you swing a bucket with a little water in a circle that goes right over your head. You find the slowest swing that keeps the water in. Do this one only if you have a balcony or open ground nearby.

materials.item: a light plastic bucket with a strong handle, with about one cup of water in it
an open outdoor space, or a bathroom floor with a drain, with nobody close by
a helper with a phone or watch to count seconds, and a grown-up

schedule.what: Guess. Swing the empty bucket in a circle. Swing it with a cup of water. Slow it down until the water just stays in.

activities.safety: A grown-up must be there. Swing only a light plastic bucket with a strong handle. Keep everyone at least 3 metres away, and make sure the floor is not slippery. Stop if you feel dizzy.
activities.record: Draw the bucket at the top of its swing, with the water inside it. Write how long one turn took when the water just stayed in.

setup.art: A girl holding a plastic bucket by its handle with her arm straight, swinging it in a circle in the air beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Swing the empty bucket in a full circle beside you.

setup.art: The bucket at the top of the circle upside down, with the water staying in it and a grown-up watching nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Add a cup of water. Swing fast. The water stays in.

setup.art: A helper counting seconds aloud with a stopwatch while the girl swings more slowly.
setup.caption: 3. Swing slower and slower. Count the seconds for one turn.

flow.do: Show the bucket and the water. Ask your child to guess what the water will do when the bucket is upside down at the top. Ask why.
flow.say: When the bucket is upside down at the top, what do you think will happen to the water? Will it fall out? What if I swing very fast?
flow.kid: The bucket goes upside down at the top. What happens to the water? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the water at the top of the swing? Why?
good: It will fall out on my head.
It will stay in if I swing fast.
It will stay in because it is pushed outward.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the water will fall out whatever the speed. Write down what your child says.
flow.context: This is the first step of Water Stays Up. You guess before you swing.

flow.do: Hold the empty bucket by its handle with your arm straight. Swing it in a full circle beside your body. Practise until the circle is smooth and the bucket does not hit you.
flow.say: Swing the empty bucket in a full circle, beside your body. Keep your arm straight. Make it smooth. Is the pull on your arm bigger at the top or at the bottom?
flow.kid: Swing the empty bucket in a full circle. Keep your arm straight. Make it smooth.
flow.parent: The circle is beside the body, in a vertical plane, not in front. Stand with feet apart. A grown-up stays at a distance. If the child cannot swing a full circle smoothly, stop and do not add water.
flow.context: In this step, you practise swinging the empty bucket in a full circle.

flow.do: Put one cup of water in the bucket. Swing it in the full circle. The helper counts the seconds for one turn. Swing more and more slowly, until the water just stays in. Then try one slightly slower, which should spill.
flow.say: Now there is a cup of water in the bucket. Swing fast and the water stays in. Swing slower and slower. Where does it start to spill? Count the seconds for one turn.
flow.kid: Swing the bucket with water. Go slower and slower. Where does it spill? Count the seconds.
flow.parent: For an arm and a bucket together about 70 centimetres long, most children find that the water just stays in when one turn takes about 1.5 to 2 seconds. Slower than that, the water falls out near the top. Do this over a drain or on open ground, and expect to get wet. Stop if the child feels dizzy.

check.q: The water stayed in the upside-down bucket when you swung fast, but fell out when you swung slowly. What is the best explanation?
options: At the top, the bucket must move downward faster than the water would fall on its own
The water became lighter when you swung fast
Fast swinging stuck the water to the bucket with glue
check.why: At the top, gravity pulls the water down. If the bucket is moving down faster than the water would fall, the bottom of the bucket stays with the water and pushes on it. If the swing is too slow, the water falls away from the bucket. The water's weight did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you find the slowest swing that keeps the water in.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: The water stayed in because the bucket was going round fast. What do you think a roller-coaster loop has in common with the bucket?
flow.kid: Why does the water stay in? What does a roller-coaster loop have in common?

ask.q: What do a swung bucket and a roller-coaster loop have in common?
good: They both go in a circle that goes upside down.
They both need enough speed at the top.
Slow and the water, or the car, falls.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: a thing in a vertical circle must go fast enough at the top, so that gravity alone does not pull it away from the track or the bucket. This is why a roller coaster has to start high, and why a loop must be built carefully.
flow.context: In this step, you link the bucket to a roller-coaster loop.

activities.title: Watch the Dryer: where do the water drops go?
activities.context: In this activity, you watch a salad spinner or a spin dryer throw water out through its holes, and you spin a wet umbrella to see where the drops go. You find out what the spin does to the water and what it does to the leaves or the clothes.

materials.item: a salad spinner with a few wet washed lettuce or coriander leaves, or the spin dryer of a washing machine with a grown-up to start it
a wet closed umbrella, and a bathroom or an open space to spin it in
a sheet of newspaper to put on the floor

schedule.what: Guess. Spin wet leaves in the spinner, or watch the dryer. Spin the wet umbrella. Say where the water goes and why.

activities.safety: A grown-up starts any machine. Never open a spin dryer or lift its lid while it is turning, and stand a metre back. Wash the leaves first. Spin the umbrella away from people and from breakable things, and mop up the water at once.
activities.record: Draw the drum or the spinner from above, with the leaves against the wall and arrows showing where the drops go. Draw the umbrella with arrows for the drops.

setup.art: A salad spinner with wet green leaves inside, being closed by a girl.
setup.caption: 1. Put the wet leaves in the spinner and close the lid.

setup.art: The salad spinner being turned, with water drops leaving through the holes of the inner basket into the outer bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Spin it. Watch where the water goes.

setup.art: A girl spinning a wet closed umbrella in a bathroom, with drops flying off in straight lines onto a newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. Spin a wet umbrella. Where do the drops land?

flow.do: Show the spinner or the dryer. Ask your child to guess what will happen to the water and to the leaves or clothes when the machine spins. Ask why.
flow.say: We will spin wet leaves. What do you think will happen to the water? What will happen to the leaves? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wet leaves in a spinner. Where does the water go? Where do the leaves go? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the water will go when the spinner turns, and why?
good: Out through the holes.
To the outside of the basket.
The water will go to the middle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Watch the Dryer. You guess before you spin.

flow.do: Spin the wet leaves in the salad spinner for about 10 seconds. Open the lid and look. See where the leaves are, and where the water has gone. If you use the washing machine, a grown-up starts the spin cycle, and you watch from a metre back.
flow.say: Spin the leaves. Now open the lid. Where are the leaves? Where is the water? What does the basket have in its wall?
flow.kid: Spin the wet leaves. Open the lid. Where are the leaves? Where is the water?
flow.parent: The leaves should be pressed against the wall of the basket and fairly dry. The water should be in the outer bowl, which it reached through the holes in the basket's wall. For a washing machine, never lift the lid or open the door while it is turning.

check.q: The water left the spinner through the holes, but the leaves stayed in. What is the best explanation?
options: The wall held the leaves in the circle, but the holes let the water go straight on
The water is lighter than the leaves
The holes sucked the water out
check.why: The wall pushes the leaves inward and holds them in the circle. Where there is a hole, nothing pushes the water inward, so the water goes straight on, through the hole. The holes do not suck, and the spin does the sorting.

flow.context: In this step, you spin wet leaves and see where the water and the leaves end up.

flow.do: Lay newspaper on the floor of the bathroom. Hold a wet closed umbrella by its handle, and spin it quickly. Look at where the drops land on the newspaper. Notice whether the marks are in a ring, or in straight lines.
flow.say: Spin the wet umbrella. The drops will fly off. Where do they land? Look at the marks on the paper. Are they in a ring, or in straight lines?
flow.kid: Spin the wet umbrella. Look at the newspaper. Are the marks in straight lines?
flow.parent: Spin the umbrella on the spot, with the tip of the umbrella pointing up and outward. The drops leave the tip in straight lines along the way the tip was moving, and so the marks on the paper form straight streaks. Mop up the water at once.
flow.context: In this step, you spin a wet umbrella and see which way the drops fly.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: In the spinner, the water got out and the leaves did not. Nobody picked out the water by hand. What did the sorting?
flow.kid: Nobody picked out the water. What did the sorting?

ask.q: What did the sorting in the spinner, if nobody picked out the water?
good: The spinning did it.
The wall holds the leaves, but the holes let the water go.
Things that are not held go straight.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: the spin does the work. Whatever is held goes round, and whatever is not held goes straight on. A cream separator and a laboratory centrifuge use the same idea, with heavier parts moving to the outside.
flow.context: In this step, you find out what does the sorting in a spinner.

projects.title: Planets on a String: do far planets go round slower?
projects.context: In this project, you use the whirler from the main experiment, and change the length of the string to see what happens to the speed of the circling. You link it to the planets in the solar system.

materials.item: the whirler from the main experiment: a plastic pen barrel, a string, a soft bag with 2 coins, and a pouch
4 one-rupee coins to put in the pouch
3 pieces of tape in different colours, and a ruler or measuring tape
a phone or watch with a stopwatch, and a helper to count turns
a clear space about 3 metres across, away from people and breakable things

projects.safety: Use only the soft bag. Whirl it in front of you at arm's length, away from faces and other people. A grown-up stays close. Keep coins away from children under five.

schedule.what: Guess. Mark the string at three lengths. Count the turns in 10 seconds for each length. Chart the results and link them to the planets.

projects.record: Make a table with three rows, one for each string length. Write the middle result of three tries for each. Draw a bar chart of the three results.

setup.art: The whirler string with three pieces of coloured tape stuck on it, at 20, 35 and 50 centimetres from the bag.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the string at 20, 35 and 50 centimetres from the bag.

setup.art: A girl whirling the bag with the red tape held at the top of the pen, while a boy counts turns with a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Whirl the bag with the first tape at the top of the pen.

setup.art: A drawing of the Sun with three planets on rings, the inner one with a short arrow and the outer one with a long arrow.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the string with the planets going round the Sun.

flow.do: Say that Mercury goes round the Sun in about 88 days, the Earth in one year and Jupiter in about 12 years. Ask for a guess and a reason about the string.
flow.say: Far planets take much longer to go round the Sun. With the whirler, the pull stays the same, but we make the string longer. Will the bag go round faster, slower or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Far planets go round slowly. A longer string, the same pull. Faster, slower, or the same? Why?

ask.q: If the string is longer and the pull is the same, will the bag go round faster, slower or the same? Why?
good: Slower, because it has a longer way to go.
Slower, because the circle is bigger.
The same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Planets on a String. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Build the whirler as before. Put 4 coins in the pouch. Stick the first tape on the string 20 centimetres from the bag. Stick the second tape at 35 centimetres, and the third at 50 centimetres.
flow.say: Use the same whirler as before. Keep 4 coins in the pouch the whole time. Three tapes mark three lengths of string above the pen.
flow.kid: Use the whirler. Keep 4 coins in the pouch. Stick on three tapes.
flow.parent: The pull is the same for every length, because the number of coins does not change. Use a different colour for each tape. If you do not have the whirler from the main experiment, build it from the steps there.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the string at three lengths.

flow.do: Whirl the bag with the 20 centimetre tape at the top of the pen. The helper counts the turns in 10 seconds. Do 3 tries. Then do the same with the 35 centimetre tape, and with the 50 centimetre tape.
flow.say: Whirl with the first tape at the top of the pen. Hold it steady. The helper counts the turns in 10 seconds. Then try the second tape, and the third.
flow.kid: Whirl with the first tape at the top. Count the turns in 10 seconds. Then try the other tapes.
flow.parent: Expect roughly 14, 11 and 9 turns in 10 seconds for the 20, 35 and 50 centimetre lengths. Your numbers will differ, but the shortest string should give the most turns. Use the middle of the three tries.

check.q: With the same pull, the bag on the longest string went round fewer times in 10 seconds. What does that tell you?
options: A bigger circle with the same pull means a slower circling
A longer string makes the bag lighter
The coins got heavier
check.why: With the same pull, a bigger circle needs a slower turn rate. The pull is shared out over a longer path. The coins and the bag did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you count the turns for three string lengths with the same pull.

flow.do: Make a table and draw a bar chart of the middle results. Ask your child to say or write a claim, evidence and reason.
flow.say: What did you find? Which length gave the most turns? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each length. Say what you found and why.

ask.q: What happened to the number of turns when the string got longer?
good: The turns got fewer.
The bag went round more slowly.
A longer string means a slower circle.

flow.context: In this step, you draw a chart and say what it shows.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first. Then read the note for the parent.
flow.say: Mercury takes about 88 days to go round the Sun. Jupiter takes about 12 years. How is that like your string?
flow.kid: Far planets take longer to go round the Sun. How is that like your string?

ask.q: How are far planets like the bag on the longer string?
good: They go round more slowly.
They have a bigger circle.
They take longer for each turn.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: in the solar system, the Sun's gravity is the pull, and it gets weaker with distance. That makes far planets even slower than your string. Mercury goes round the Sun in about 88 days, the Earth in one year, Jupiter in about 12 years, and Neptune in about 165 years.
flow.context: In this step, you link your result to the planets going round the Sun.

challenges.title: The Coin Keeper: keep three coins on a plate at one turn a second
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a turntable surface that keeps three coins on it while it turns once every second, with the coins starting at the edge. The plate that keeps its coins at the fastest speed wins.
challenges.problem: Make a plate that keeps three coins on it, starting at 15 centimetres from the middle, while the turntable turns once every second for 5 turns. Make it keep the coins at as fast a speed as you can.
constraints: The three coins must start on the ring 15 centimetres from the middle.
You may change the plate's surface, tilt it, or add a rim. You may not tape, glue or stick the coins down.
The turntable must turn once every second, counted aloud, for 5 turns.
The coins must all stay on the plate for the whole test.
Test it 3 times, and the best of the three counts.
materials: a turntable you can turn by hand and a flat steel plate, as in the Coins on the Turntable test
pieces of rough cloth, sandpaper, a rubber mat or shelf lining, a towel, and a sheet of smooth plastic
cardboard strips for a rim, tape, and scissors
a helper to turn the turntable and count aloud
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the cardboard and any sandpaper. Stand a metre back from the turntable, because a coin can fly off. Keep coins away from children under five.
general: Put a rough surface on the plate, such as a rubber mat or sandpaper, to give more friction.
Cover the plate with a towel or a cloth, so the coins grip.
Use a plate whose surface is more sticky than a smooth steel thali.
creative: Add a low cardboard rim round the edge of the plate. The rim can push the coins inward, and the push does not depend on friction.
Tilt the plate into a shallow dish shape, by laying a bowl under a rubber mat, so the dish wall pushes the coins inward.
Raise the plate's outer edge a little, so the coins lean inward towards the middle.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plate. Build it and test it 3 times at one turn every second. Change one thing, and test again. Which change worked best? Why do you think it did?

setup.caption: 1. Sketch some plate designs on paper.

setup.art: A plate with a cardboard rim taped round its edge and three coins on the 15 centimetre ring, on a swivel stool seat.
setup.caption: 2. Build your plate, and put three coins on the outer ring.

setup.art: A helper turning the seat with a count of one turn every second, while the child watches the three coins stay on.
setup.caption: 3. Turn it once every second for 5 turns. Do the coins stay on?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three plate designs.
flow.say: The coins start at the edge, and the plate must turn once every second. How could you stop the coins sliding off? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Coins at the edge. A fast turn. How can you keep them on? Draw some ideas.

ask.q: What would stop a coin from sliding off a fast turntable?
good: More friction, so the plate grips the coin.
A wall at the edge, to push the coin inward.
A dish shape, so the plate tilts the coin inward.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Keeper challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Put it on the turntable. Put three coins on the ring at 15 centimetres. Check that the plate is centred on the turntable.
flow.say: Build your first plate. Put the three coins on the outer ring. Check that the plate is centred. Then it is ready to test.
flow.kid: Build your plate. Put three coins on the outer ring. Check that it is in the middle of the turntable.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the cardboard and sandpaper. The plate must be centred on the turntable, or the test is unfair. Fix the plate to the turntable if it slides.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design.

flow.do: The helper turns the turntable once every second for 5 turns, counting aloud. Note how many coins stay on. Change one thing, such as the surface or the rim. Test again 3 times.
flow.say: Turn the plate once every second, and count aloud. Do all three coins stay on? If not, change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Turn once every second. Do all three coins stay on? Change one thing and try again.
flow.parent: Change only one thing at a time, or you will not know which change helped. A rough surface alone often keeps the coins on at a slow turn. A rim or a dish shape usually does best at a fast turn, because a wall pushes the coin inward whatever the friction.

check.q: A cardboard rim round the edge of the plate kept the coins on at a fast turn. What is the best explanation?
options: The rim pushed the coins inward, so the plate did not need friction to hold them
The rim made the coins lighter
The rim made the plate turn slower
check.why: A thing going round needs a push towards the middle. Friction can give it. A rim can give it as well, as a wall does for the clothes in a dryer. The coins and the speed did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you test your design and improve it with one change at a time.

flow.do: Compare designs. Ask which change helped most. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which change worked best? What does that tell you about the pull towards the middle?
flow.kid: Which change worked best? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which change worked best, and where did the pull towards the middle come from?
good: The rim worked best, because the wall gave the pull.
A rough mat worked, because friction gave the pull.
A dish shape worked, because the slope gave an inward push.

flow.context: In this step, you compare designs and say what gave the pull towards the middle.

items.p: Priya whirls a stone on a string, and the string snaps. Which way does the stone go?
opts: Straight on, along the way it was moving
Straight outward, away from her hand
Round in a curve
items.why: When the pull stops, nothing bends the stone's path. It goes straight on, along the line that just touches the circle. Picking 'outward' is the most common mix-up: the stone does not go along the string.

items.p: A force that points towards the middle of a circle and keeps a thing going round is called the ____ force.
a: centripetal
items.why: Centripetal means centre-seeking. It is not a new kind of force. It is the name for whatever pull or push points to the middle, such as a string, friction or gravity.

items.p: Karthik says, 'When you let go of a whirled stone, it flies outward along the string.' Is he right?
items.why: False. The stone goes straight on, along the way it was moving at that moment, which is at a right angle to the string. Your fingers felt the stone pulling outward on the string, but the stone itself was never pushed outward.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Radius
the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge
Tangent
a straight line that just touches a circle
Centripetal force
a pull towards the middle of the circle
Turn
one full trip round a circle
Orbit
the path of one thing going round another because of gravity
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each, such as the Moon for orbit and sparks from a grinding wheel for tangent.

items.p: Divya lists six things that go round. Sort each one by what gives the pull towards the middle.
items: A bag whirled on a string
A car on a flat bend
The Moon going round the Earth
A coin on a turning plate
A hammer on a wire, before it is thrown
A satellite going round the Earth
items.why: Whatever goes round needs a pull towards the middle, and something has to give it. A string gives tension, tyres and plates give friction, and the Earth gives gravity. A strong answer can say what would happen to each thing if its pull stopped.

items.p: A bag goes round 12 times in 10 seconds. How many turns does it make in 30 seconds, if it keeps the same pace?
items.why: 30 seconds is 3 times as long as 10 seconds. 12 times 3 is 36 turns.

items.p: A stone is whirled on a string in a circle. The stone is whirled twice as fast in the same circle. How does the pull needed change?
opts: It becomes twice as big
It becomes four times as big
It stays the same
items.why: The pull grows with the square of the speed. Twice the speed needs 2 times 2, which is 4 times the pull. Picking 'twice as big' is the natural guess, and it is the one the whirler test showed was too small.

items.p: Put the steps of the Whirler test in order.
items: Count the turns in 10 seconds with each number of coins
Guess how the turns will change with more coins
Build the whirler with the pen, string, bag and pouch
Practise until the tape stays steady
Say what you found and why
a: Guess how the turns will change with more coins
Build the whirler with the pen, string, bag and pouch
Practise until the tape stays steady
Count the turns in 10 seconds with each number of coins
Say what you found and why
items.why: First guess, so the test can surprise you. Then build and practise, count with each number of coins, and last say what you found and why.

items.p: In the Whirler test, four times the coins made the bag go round only about twice as fast. Explain why four times the pull does not make it four times as fast.
items.a: A faster circle needs a pull that grows with the square of the speed. Twice the speed needs four times the pull, so four times the pull only makes the bag go about twice as fast.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pull grows with the square of the speed, so the speed grows more slowly than the pull.

items.p: Three of these happen because a thing goes straight on when its pull stops. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Sparks leave a grinding wheel
Mud flies off a fast tyre
Drops fly from a spun wet umbrella
The Moon keeps going round the Earth
items.why: The Moon is still being pulled by the Earth's gravity, so it keeps going round. In the other three, the pull that held the spark, the mud or the drop was too small, so each of them went straight on.

items.p: Here is a picture of a bag whirled on a string. Label the four parts.
labels: the straight line the bag would take if the string snapped
a: the bag: the thing going round
the string: gives the pull towards the middle
the hand at the middle: the centre of the circle
the straight line: along the way the bag was moving at that moment
items.why: The string gives the pull that holds the bag in its circle. If the string snapped, the bag would go along the straight line that just touches the circle.
items.art: A top view of a small bag on a string going round a hand in a circle, with a straight dotted line touching the circle at the bag, and four empty label boxes.

items.p: In a spin dryer, why do the clothes stay in the drum while the water leaves?
opts: The wall holds the clothes in the circle, but the holes let the water go straight on
The water is lighter than the clothes
The holes suck the water out
items.why: The wall pushes the clothes inward and keeps them in the circle. Where there is a hole, nothing holds the water, so it goes straight on and leaves. Nothing sucks.

items.p: Coins sit on a plate that turns faster and faster. Which coin slides off first?
opts: The coin nearest the edge
The coin nearest the middle
The heaviest coin
items.why: The coin at the edge goes round the biggest circle and moves fastest, so it needs the biggest pull from friction. Weight does not settle it, because a heavier coin is also gripped harder.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru talk about a bus turning left.

views.says: I felt a push throwing me to the outside when the bus turned. Some force must be pushing me outward.
Nobody pushed you outward. Your body kept going straight and the bus turned. The window pushed you inward.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about a thing going straight. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Imran: the body's inertia keeps it going straight, and the window gives the inward push that bends its path. It is fair to Pooja: she really did feel pressed against the window, and the feeling is real. Many engineers call that feeling centrifugal force, and scientists still discuss how to describe it.
items.why: Both children describe the same thing. What differs is whether the outward feeling is a force on the body, or the body's own tendency to go straight.

items.p: Draw a stone going round on a string. Mark the point where the string snaps, and draw the straight path the stone takes afterwards.
items.a: A circle with a stone on it, and a straight line leaving the circle at the point where the string snaps, touching the circle.
items.why: After the string snaps, the stone goes along the way it was moving, so its path is a straight line that just touches the circle. A strong drawing does not show the line going outward from the middle.
items.art: A circle drawn on paper with a dot at the middle, a stone on the circle, and space beside it for the child to draw a straight path.

items.p: A car takes a bend on a wet road and slides straight off the road. What is the best explanation?
opts: The tyres did not have enough grip to give the pull towards the middle
The car became heavier on the bend
The road pulled the car outward
items.why: On a flat bend, friction gives the pull towards the middle. A wet road gives less friction, so the car could not be held in the curve and went straight on.

items.p: The pull needed to hold a stone in a circle is the mass times the speed times the speed, divided by the radius. A stone of 0.5 kilograms goes round at 4 metres per second on a string 2 metres long. What is the pull, in newtons?
items.why: 0.5 times 4 times 4 is 8. 8 divided by 2 is 4. The pull is 4 newtons.

items.p: A stone of 0.5 kilograms needs a pull of 4 newtons to go round at 4 metres per second on a string 2 metres long. How many newtons does it need at 8 metres per second on the same string?
items.why: Twice the speed needs four times the pull. 4 times 4 is 16. The pull is 16 newtons.

items.p: A bag needs a pull of 3 newtons to go round at a steady speed in a circle. It is whirled twice as fast in the same circle. What pull does it need now?
opts: 6 newtons
12 newtons
9 newtons
items.why: Twice the speed needs four times the pull. 3 times 4 is 12. Picking 6 doubles the pull when the speed doubles, and forgets that the pull grows with the square of the speed.

items.p: A stone on a 1 metre string needs a pull of 8 newtons at a certain speed. The string is replaced by one 2 metres long, and the stone goes at the same speed. What pull does it need?
opts: 4 newtons
8 newtons
16 newtons
items.why: A circle that is twice as wide needs half the pull at the same speed. Half of 8 is 4. Picking 16 reverses the rule.

items.p: Heena says, 'A heavy coin and a light coin at the same distance from the middle of a turntable slide off at the same speed of turning.' Is she right?
items.why: True. A heavier coin needs a bigger pull, but it also presses harder on the plate, so the friction that holds it grows in the same proportion. The two cancel, and only the distance and the roughness of the plate matter.

items.p: Sort each change: does it make the pull needed bigger or smaller?
items: The same bag whirled twice as fast
The same bag in a circle twice as wide, at the same speed
A heavier bag at the same speed in the same circle
A car taking the same bend at half the speed
A coin moved from the edge of a turntable to the middle, with the turntable turning at the same rate
A lorry in place of a car, at the same speed on the same bend
items.why: More speed, more mass and a tighter circle all need a bigger pull. A slower speed, a wider circle and a smaller mass need a smaller pull. A coin near the middle goes round a smaller circle and moves more slowly.

items.p: A machine that spins things fast, so that heavier parts move to the outside, is called a ____.
a: centrifuge
items.why: A centrifuge spins a mixture, so the heavier parts move to the outer end and the lighter parts stay nearer the middle. Hospitals use them to separate blood.

items.p: The Moon keeps going round the Earth and never crashes into it. What is the best explanation?
opts: It keeps falling towards the Earth, but it moves sideways fast enough to keep missing
It is too far away for gravity to reach
It is held up by the air
items.why: Gravity pulls the Moon towards the Earth all the time. The Moon also moves sideways at about 1 kilometre every second, so as it falls, the Earth's surface curves away. It keeps missing. Gravity does reach the Moon, and there is no air to hold it.

items.p: A car takes a bend at 60 kilometres an hour. The driver slows to 30 kilometres an hour. How does the grip needed from the tyres change? Explain.
items.a: The grip needed becomes one quarter as big. Half the speed needs one quarter of the pull towards the middle, because the pull grows with the square of the speed. That is why slowing down for a bend helps so much.
items.why: A strong answer says that the grip needed falls to one quarter, and links it to the square of the speed.

items.p: Draw a cyclist taking a bend to the left. Show which way the cyclist leans, and draw an arrow for the push of the ground on the cycle.
items.a: A cyclist leaning to the left, towards the inside of the bend, with an arrow from the ground pointing inward and up through the cycle.
items.why: A cyclist leans into the bend, so that the push of the ground points towards the middle of the turn. The faster the speed or the tighter the bend, the more the cyclist leans.
items.art: A back view of a girl on a cycle on a flat road, upright, with space to the left and right for the child to draw the lean and an arrow.

items.p: Two friends in Pune talk about the Moon.

views.says: The Moon floats up there because it is so far away that there is no gravity.
There is gravity. The Moon keeps falling towards the Earth, but it keeps missing, because it is moving sideways.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about a thing going round. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Sana: gravity holds the Moon in its ring, and if it stopped, the Moon would fly off in a straight line. It is fair to Neel: the Moon is far away and its pull is much weaker there, about 3,600 times weaker than at the ground, and astronauts in space do feel weightless because they are falling together with their spacecraft.
items.why: Neel has noticed that gravity is weaker far away and that astronauts float, which is true. But weaker is not zero. The Moon needs a pull towards the middle, and gravity gives it.

items.p: Match each moving thing to what gives its pull towards the middle.
pairs: A whirled bag
the tension in the string
A car on a flat bend
the friction between tyres and road
The Moon
the Earth's gravity
Clothes in a spin dryer
the push of the drum wall
A rider on a giant wheel
the push of the seat and the safety bar
items.why: Whatever goes round needs a pull towards the middle. In each case something different supplies it, but its job is the same.

items.p: A bucket of water is swung in a circle over a person's head, and the water stays in at the top. This happens only if
opts: the bucket is moving downward faster than the water would fall
the water is very cold
the bucket is pushed up by the air
items.why: At the top, the bucket's bottom must push down on the water faster than gravity alone would. If it moved more slowly, the water would fall away from it.

items.p: A bag makes 5 turns in 10 seconds. How many seconds does it take for one turn?
items.why: 10 seconds divided by 5 turns is 2 seconds for one turn.

items.p: A cream separator spins milk. Where does the cream, the lighter part, gather?
opts: Nearer the middle
At the outer wall
It stays evenly spread through the milk
items.why: The heavier watery milk is pushed to the outside, and the lighter cream gathers nearer the middle. The two can then leave through different pipes.

items.p: Here is a top view of a bus turning left with a passenger standing in it. Label what each arrow shows.
labels: the arrow pointing straight ahead from the passenger
the arrow from the window pointing inward
the curved arrow of the bus
a: the arrow pointing straight ahead: the way the passenger's body wants to go
the arrow from the window: the push of the window on the passenger
the curved arrow: the path the bus takes as it turns
the passenger: pressed against the window on the outside of the turn
items.why: The passenger's body wants to go straight on. The window pushes inward, and bends the passenger's path into the turn. The pressing feeling is the passenger's own body pressing on the window.
items.art: A top view of a bus turning left with a passenger pressed against the right window, and four empty label boxes beside arrows.

items.p: Three of these need a pull towards the middle all the time. Which one does not?
opts: The Moon going round the Earth
A car taking a bend
A coin sliding straight off a turntable
A stone whirled on a string
items.why: A coin sliding straight off has lost its pull towards the middle, so it goes straight on. The other three are going round, and each needs a pull towards the middle at every moment.

items.p: The pull needed is the mass times the speed times the speed, divided by the radius. A child of 40 kilograms sits at the edge of a roundabout of radius 2 metres, going at 3 metres per second. How many newtons of holding force does the child need?
items.why: 40 times 3 times 3 is 360. 360 divided by 2 is 180. The child needs 180 newtons.

items.p: A stone of 1 kilogram needs a pull of 9 newtons on a string 1 metre long, at a certain speed. How many newtons does it need on a string 3 metres long, at the same speed?
items.why: A circle 3 times as wide needs one third of the pull at the same speed. 9 divided by 3 is 3 newtons.

items.p: A road bend is rebuilt in a circle twice as wide, with the same speed limit. What is the effect on the grip each car needs?
opts: It needs half as much grip
It needs the same grip
It needs twice as much grip
items.why: A circle twice as wide needs half the pull at the same speed. That is one reason why road builders try to make bends wide.

items.p: In a spin dryer, the drum wall pushes the water outward through the holes. True or false?
items.why: False. The wall pushes the clothes inward, which holds them in the circle. The wall does not push the water. Where there are holes, nothing holds the water, so it goes straight on and leaves.

items.p: On a bus bend, you feel pressed against the window on the outside. Explain what is really happening, using the words 'inertia' and 'inward'.
items.a: Your body has inertia, so it keeps going straight while the bus turns. The window pushes you inward, which bends your path into the turn. The feeling of being pressed outward is your own body pressing on the window.
items.why: A strong answer says that the body tries to go straight, that the window pushes it inward, and that the outward feeling is the body pressing on the window.

items.p: Two friends in Guwahati talk about a coin that slides off a spinning plate.

views.says: The coin flew off because a force pushed it away from the middle.
Nothing pushed it away. The friction was too small to hold it in the circle, so it went straight on.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you found with the coins on the turntable. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Rohit, using evidence: the coin at the edge slid off first, because friction was not enough to give the pull it needed, and the coin went straight on. It is fair to Mina: in the spinning plate, things do seem to be pushed outward, and engineers use the idea of a centrifugal force to describe it.
items.why: Both friends describe what happens on a spinning plate. Rohit describes it as seen from outside, where nothing pushes outward. Mina describes it as it appears from the plate.

items.p: A satellite goes round the Earth at a steady speed. If the Earth's gravity suddenly vanished, what would the satellite do?
opts: Go off in a straight line
Fall straight down
Keep going round in a circle
items.why: Gravity is the pull that bends the satellite's path into a circle. With it gone, the satellite would go straight on, along the way it was moving.

items.p: The same stone goes round on the same string at three speeds. Put the speeds in order, from the one that needs the smallest pull to the one that needs the biggest.
a: 1 metre per second
2 metres per second
3 metres per second
items.why: The pull grows with the square of the speed. At 1 metre per second the pull is 1 unit, at 2 it is 4 units and at 3 it is 9 units.

items.p: A wet umbrella is spinning, with its rim going round anticlockwise. Draw the umbrella from above, and show the path of a drop of water as it leaves the rim.
items.a: A circle for the umbrella, and a drop leaving the rim along a straight line that touches the circle, in the direction the rim was moving.
items.why: The drop goes straight on, along the way the rim was moving at that moment. Its path is a straight line that touches the circle, not a spoke going outward.
items.art: An umbrella seen from above as a circle with spokes, and a blank space beside the rim for the child to draw the path of a drop.

items.p: Does each thing keep going round, or go straight on?
items: A satellite with the Earth's pull still on it
A coin that has just lost its grip on a turntable
Clothes in a spin dryer, held by the wall
A hammer after the thrower lets go
A car on a bend with enough grip
items.why: A thing keeps going round only while the pull towards the middle is enough. When the pull stops or is not enough, the thing goes straight on.

items.p: A hospital centrifuge spins a tube of blood. Where do the heavier blood cells gather?
opts: At the outer end of the tube
Near the middle
At the top of the liquid
items.why: The heavier cells need more pull to stay in the circle, so they move to the outside. In the tube, the outside is the bottom end. The lighter liquid stays above.

items.p: In a circle, the distance from the centre to the edge is called the ____.
a: radius
items.why: The radius tells you how tight or wide the circle is. A string 40 centimetres long makes a circle with a radius of 40 centimetres.

items.p: A giant wheel turns steadily. At which point does a rider feel lightest?
opts: At the top
At the bottom
At the side
items.why: At the top, the seat has to push up less than the rider's weight, because part of the weight is used to give the pull towards the middle. At the bottom, the seat must push up more.

items.p: Gravity pulls the Moon all the time, but the Moon never gets closer. Explain how it can keep falling and never arrive.
items.a: The Moon is moving sideways very fast as well as being pulled towards the Earth. As it falls, the Earth's surface curves away beneath it, so it keeps missing the Earth. It falls round the Earth instead of into it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the Moon has a sideways speed, and that the pull bends its path round the Earth, so it keeps falling and keeps missing.

items.p: Here is a picture of a cannon on a very tall mountain, firing three balls. Label the three paths.
labels: the ball fired fast enough to go right round the Earth
a: the slowest ball: lands close to the mountain
a faster ball: lands further away
the ball fired fast enough: keeps missing the Earth and goes round it
items.why: Newton imagined faster and faster shots. A slow ball falls near. A faster ball lands further. A ball fast enough keeps falling but the ground curves away, so it never lands. That is an orbit.
items.art: A very tall mountain on a small globe with a cannon on top, and three curved paths, one landing near, one landing further, and one going right round.

items.p: A satellite goes round the Earth once every 90 minutes. How many times does it go round in 24 hours?
items.why: 24 hours is 24 times 60, which is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 90 is 16 times.

quiz.p: A thing that was going round in a circle suddenly has nothing pulling it towards the middle. What does it do next?
opts: It goes straight on, along the way it was moving
It goes outward from the middle
It stops at once
quiz.why: With no pull, nothing bends the path, so the thing goes straight on. It does not go outward along the radius, and it does not stop.

quiz.p: What is needed to keep a thing going round in a circle?
opts: A pull towards the middle, all the time
A push forward, all the time
A push outward, all the time
quiz.why: The pull towards the middle bends the path round. A forward push would change the speed, and an outward push would make the thing leave the circle.

quiz.p: In the Whirler test, what happened as more coins were hung on the string?
opts: The bag had to go round faster
The bag could go round more slowly
The bag went round at the same speed
quiz.why: More coins mean a bigger pull on the string, and the bag must go round faster to hold the same circle. The speed went up more slowly than the pull.

quiz.p: A car goes through a bend at 20 kilometres an hour, and then through the same bend at 40 kilometres an hour. How does the grip the tyres need change?
opts: It needs four times as much grip
It needs twice as much grip
It needs the same grip
quiz.why: Twice the speed needs four times the pull towards the middle. A small rise in speed can be too much for a bend.

quiz.p: A bag is whirled at a steady speed in a circle. It is replaced by a bag that is twice as heavy, and whirled at the same speed in the same circle. What happens to the pull needed?
opts: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
quiz.why: A bigger mass needs a bigger pull in the same proportion. Twice the mass needs twice the pull.

quiz.p: Coins sit at different distances from the middle of a turntable that turns faster and faster. Which coin slides off last?
opts: The one nearest the middle
The one nearest the edge
The heaviest one
quiz.why: Nearer the middle, the circle is smaller and the coin moves more slowly, so it needs less friction. It stays on the longest.

quiz.p: In a cream separator, the heavier part of the milk moves to the ____ of the spinning bowl.
a: outside
outer wall
edge
quiz.why: The heavier watery milk is pushed to the outside, and the lighter cream gathers nearer the middle.

quiz.p: In a spin dryer, what lets the water leave the clothes?
opts: The holes let the water go straight on, while the wall holds the clothes
The drum squeezes the clothes dry
The lid sucks the water up
quiz.why: The wall holds the clothes in the circle, and the holes let the water go. The spin does the sorting.

quiz.p: Why are railway curves built with the outer rail a little higher than the inner rail?
opts: So that part of the push of the rails points towards the middle of the curve
So that the train goes faster

quiz.p: A bag makes 24 turns in 20 seconds. How many turns does it make in 10 seconds, at the same pace?

applications: Spin dryers and salad spinners dry clothes and leaves by letting the water go straight on through the holes.
Dairies use cream separators, and hospitals use centrifuges to separate blood cells from the liquid in blood.
Road and railway engineers tilt bends and set speed limits, so vehicles can take them safely.
Cyclists, motorcyclists and skiers lean into turns, so that the push of the ground points towards the middle.
Engineers design giant wheels, merry-go-rounds and roller-coaster loops with the pull in mind, so that riders are held safely.
Potters set the speed of the wheel to suit the width of the pot, because clay at the edge needs more grip.
Satellites for weather, television, phones and navigation, launched by ISRO and other space agencies, are put into orbits at the speed that matches their height.
Pilots and astronauts train in big centrifuges, to get used to strong pulls when a spacecraft or plane turns or speeds up.
Hammer and discus throwers in athletics spin round, and let go at the moment when the hammer or discus points where they want it to go.
Fan blades, flywheels and grinding wheels are made strong enough to hold themselves in the circle, because the pull needed grows with the square of the speed.

open_questions.q: Why do almost all the things in space spin?
open_questions.why_open: Stars, planets and galaxies nearly all spin. Scientists know that a cloud of gas spins faster as it shrinks, but exactly how the first spin began in the early universe is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: When something spins, what is the spin measured against?
open_questions.why_open: Newton thought the spin of a bucket of water shows spin in empty space. Ernst Mach thought it might be spin against the far-away stars. Nobody has settled the question.

open_questions.q: Is gravity a pull, or a bend in space and time?
open_questions.why_open: Einstein's theory describes gravity as a bend in space and time, and it has passed every test so far. Newton's idea of a pull gives the same answers for everyday things. A theory that joins gravity with quantum physics is still missing.

open_questions.q: How fast can a star spin before it breaks apart?
open_questions.why_open: Some small, dense stars called pulsars spin hundreds of times every second. Scientists are still finding out how fast a star can possibly spin and what holds it together.

open_questions.q: Could people live in a big spinning space town, and would it be comfortable?
open_questions.why_open: The science is clear that a spinning ring can give a feeling like weight. But nobody has built a large one, and scientists are still working out how people would feel in one.

open_questions.q: Do the tiny particles inside atoms go round like tiny planets?
open_questions.why_open: No. Quantum physics describes them in a different way, and it does not give them simple circular paths. How to picture them is still debated.

maths.problem: In the made-up example for the Whirler test, the middle results for 4, 8 and 16 coins were 9, 13 and 18 turns in 10 seconds. How many more turns did 16 coins give than 4 coins? How many times as many coins is 16 than 4? About how many times as many turns is 18 than 9?
maths.answer: 9 more turns. 16 coins is 4 times as many as 4 coins. 18 turns is 2 times as many as 9 turns.
maths.explain: 18 take away 9 is 9. 16 divided by 4 is 4. 18 divided by 9 is 2. Four times the coins gave only twice the turns. That is the sign that the pull grows with the square of the speed.
maths.context: This is about the Whirler test. A bag goes round on a string while coins hang from the other end, and you count the turns.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how many times bigger the coins and the turns are shows a pattern that the plain numbers hide.

maths.problem: A bag makes 13 turns in 10 seconds. How many turns would it make in 1 minute, at the same pace? About how many seconds does one turn take, to the nearest tenth of a second?
maths.answer: 78 turns in a minute. One turn takes about 0.8 seconds.
maths.explain: 1 minute is 6 times 10 seconds. 13 times 6 is 78. One turn takes 10 divided by 13 seconds, which is about 0.77. To the nearest tenth, that is 0.8 seconds.
maths.context: This is about counting turns in the Whirler test, where you count how many turns the bag makes in 10 seconds.
maths.why_maths: Changing turns in 10 seconds to turns in a minute, or seconds for one turn, lets you compare whirls timed in different ways.

maths.problem: A stone needs a pull of 4 newtons to go round at 2 metres per second on a string. The pull grows with the square of the speed. What pull does it need at 1, 3 and 4 metres per second? What kind of numbers are 1, 4, 9 and 16?
maths.answer: 1 newton at 1 metre per second, 9 newtons at 3 metres per second, 16 newtons at 4 metres per second. They are square numbers.
maths.explain: At 2 metres per second the pull is 4, which is 2 times 2. At 1 it is 1 times 1, which is 1. At 3 it is 3 times 3, which is 9. At 4 it is 4 times 4, which is 16. The pull is the speed times itself, so the numbers 1, 4, 9 and 16 are square numbers.
maths.context: This is about how the pull needed grows when the speed grows, as you found in the Whirler test.
maths.why_maths: Square numbers are exactly the pattern of pulls, so the maths tells you how much pull a faster circle needs.

maths.problem: A car needs a grip of 5 units to take a bend at 10 kilometres an hour. The grip needed grows with the square of the speed. How much grip does it need at 20, 30 and 40 kilometres an hour?
maths.answer: 20 units at 20 kilometres an hour, 45 units at 30, and 80 units at 40.
maths.explain: At 20 kilometres an hour the speed is 2 times as big, so the grip is 2 times 2, which is 4 times 5, which is 20. At 30, it is 3 times 3, which is 9 times 5, which is 45. At 40, it is 4 times 4, which is 16 times 5, which is 80.
maths.context: This is about how a car on a bend needs more grip when it goes faster.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by the square of the speed shows how fast the grip needed climbs, and why a small rise in speed can be too much for a bend.

maths.problem: A satellite goes round the Earth once every 90 minutes. How many times does it go round in 3 hours? How many times in one day of 24 hours?
maths.answer: 2 times in 3 hours, and 16 times in a day.
maths.explain: 3 hours is 180 minutes. 180 divided by 90 is 2. A day is 24 times 60, which is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 90 is 16.
maths.context: This is about the Moon and satellites falling round the Earth, and how many turns they make in a given time.
maths.why_maths: Changing hours to minutes and dividing lets you count the turns of a thing that goes round, just as you counted the turns of the bag.

maths.problem: A turntable turns once every 2 seconds. What fraction of a turn does it make in 1 second? How many turns does it make in 3 seconds?
maths.answer: One half of a turn in 1 second. One and a half turns in 3 seconds.
maths.explain: One turn takes 2 seconds, so in 1 second it makes half a turn. In 3 seconds, that is 3 halves, which is 1 and a half turns.
maths.context: This is about the Coins on the Turntable test, where the helper turns the plate at a set pace.
maths.why_maths: Fractions of a turn let you describe the pace of a turntable and check that the helper keeps to it.

maths.problem: The Earth takes 1 year to go round the Sun, and Jupiter takes about 12 years. How many times does the Earth go round while Jupiter goes round 3 times? Why do far planets take longer?
maths.answer: The Earth goes round 36 times. Far planets have a bigger circle to travel and a weaker pull from the Sun, so they go round more slowly.
maths.explain: 3 times 12 is 36 years, and the Earth goes round once every year, so 36 times. The bag on the longer string also went round more slowly in the Planets on a String project.
maths.context: This is about the Planets on a String project, where the bag on a longer string goes round more slowly.
maths.why_maths: A ratio compares how often two planets go round, and shows how much slower a far planet is.

maths.problem: A coin on a turntable moves through a quarter of a turn, and then through a half of a turn more. What angle has it turned through in all? How many right angles is that?
maths.explain: A quarter of a turn is 90 degrees. A half of a turn is 180 degrees. 90 plus 180 is 270 degrees. A right angle is 90 degrees, so 270 divided by 90 is 3 right angles.
maths.context: This is about the Coins on the Turntable test. The coin goes round the middle, and the turntable turns through part of a circle.
maths.why_maths: Angles describe how far a turntable has turned, even when it has not made a whole turn.

how_we_found_out.context: Is going round in a circle natural, or does it need a cause? This card tells how people found out, and how a stone in a sling helped.
how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many thinkers followed Aristotle in saying that the heavens move in circles because circles are perfect and natural. They said a circular motion needs no cause. Even the great Galileo, in 1632, seems to have thought that circular motion could go on by itself. In 1644, René Descartes looked at a stone whirled in a sling. He saw that the stone always tries to fly off in a straight line, and that the sling must keep pulling it back. So going in a circle is not natural. It needs a pull. In 1659, Christiaan Huygens worked out how big the pull must be. Then Isaac Newton asked what pulls the Moon. The Moon is about 60 times as far from the Earth's middle as an apple on the ground. He showed that the pull weakens with the square of the distance, so it is about 3,600 times weaker there, and that fits the Moon's motion.
how_we_found_out.who: René Descartes, a French thinker, Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, and Isaac Newton, an English scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1644 for Descartes's sling, 1659 for Huygens's rule, and the 1680s for Newton's Moon
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle and many thinkers after him taught that moving in circles is natural for heavenly things, and needs no cause. A stone in a sling showed that a thing in a circle is always trying to go straight, so something must pull it inward all the time.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Whirler needs a plastic pen barrel, a string, a soft bag of two coins, a pouch of up to 16 coins, tape, and a clear space about 3 metres across, and it is the fiddliest test in the unit, so the steps include a practice step and what to do if the bag hangs low or the string rubs. The numbers were worked out from the physics for a bag of about 10 grams on a string 50 centimetres long: roughly 9, 13 and 18 turns in 10 seconds for 4, 8 and 16 coins. Hand counting and friction in the pen will change them, which is why every setting is done three times. The pattern to look for is that four times the coins needs only about twice the turns. Coins on the Turntable needs a turntable you can turn by hand, such as a swivel stool or a lazy Susan, and a smooth plate. If every coin slides at once, the plate is too smooth, and if none slides, it is too rough. Water Stays Up is for an adult-led session outdoors or on a bathroom floor, and is not in the core path. The Watch the Dryer activity needs a salad spinner or a washing machine and a grown-up. Marble in the Kadai is quick and works with any wide bowl. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 90 minutes. Facts to verify before release: the Moon's distance of about 60 Earth radii and the weakening by 3,600 times; Galileo's view of circular motion; the 1659 and 1703 dates for Huygens; the 90 minute and 8 kilometres per second figures for the Space Station; the Rig Veda 1.164.11 and Tao Te Ching 11 wording.
